speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 17 last, while I was away from this house on account of illness, the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Drouin) took advantage of that fact to behave childishly and indulge in silly remarks about me, besides insulting me.
As can be seen on page 2292 of Hansard, besides holding me responsible for a misprint in the Canadian Parliamentary Guide, he even accused me of trying to give myself out as a Liberal.
The insult is too great and my dignity as Social Credit member for Shefford riding demands a reparation.
As regards the misprint in the Parliamentary Guide, I should point out to the hon. member that as early as May 17, I sent a letter to Mr. Pierre G. Normandin, to make him aware of the misprint that had slipped into the French version of my biography.
I have here an acknowledgment of that letter from Mr. Normandin, who gives me the assurance that the error will be rectified in the guide supplement. I have that supplement in my hand and it can be seen on page 21 that the editor carried out my request and rectified the awkward error which had crept in.
The hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes lacked judgment when he thought that I could be responsible for an error committed by a printer. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask him to withdraw his remarks.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: NUCLEAR TEST BAN-ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIALLING OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house will welcome the agreement which was initialled today in Moscow for the cessation of nuclear tests in the atmosphere, in outer space and under water. This achievement, when it comes into force after signature, will be of the greatest importance not only in removing a major source of harmful radiation but because of the prospect it holds out for further improvement in east-west relations. The participants in the Moscow negotiations are deserving of our deep gratitude and our warm congratulations.
Despite the optimism which has justifiably been generated by the agreement concluded in Moscow, it would be unrealistic to ignore the fact that it is no more than a first step in the direction of the much more basic accord which will be needed to ensure world peace and security. We have still to remove the difficulties which stand in the way of a more comprehensive test ban, including underground tests. It is imperative, moreover, to ensure that any such agreement will command world wide support. Indeed, it will require universal acceptance if it is to be truly effective.
Moreover, even in agreeing to a comprehensive test ban binding on all states, we shall have dealt only with one small segment of the problems involved in working out a program of general disarmament and effective methods for the peaceful settlement of disputes. To accomplish this complex task will require prolonged and patient effort. We must not allow the present atmosphere of success to mislead us into thinking that it will be easily or quickly achieved.
At the same time we should in no way underestimate the importance of this unprecedented first step. It not only provides the momentum for further advances, but demonstrates that they are feasible and can be achieved through the realization of a common interest and by a concerted and determined effort. Significant changes in the thinking of the Soviet leaders, of which there are signs, could hold out still greater prospects for a far reaching east-west settlement.
A balanced appraisal of the present international situation should not for a momer'

Nuclear Test Ban Agreement suggest that all barriers to a genuine detente are down. It would be naive and even dangerous to have any such illusions. But what has happened does make plain that no one can afford to ignore any opportunity to press forward with negotiations aimed at a broader international understanding. So far as this government is concerned, and indeed I think it would be true of any Canadian government, we shall use to the utmost whatever influence and power we can bring to bear in assisting the speediest possible realization of this objective.
I understand that the present treaty will be open to all states, and it is to be hoped that the original signatories will make every effort to encourage the widest possible participation. I wish to assure the house that for its part the Canadian government is ready now to become a party to the agreement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: NUCLEAR TEST BAN-ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIALLING OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there will be general agreement in this house with the announcement made by the Prime Minister. My one regret on this occasion is that the former member on this side of the house who contributed so much in his courageous efforts on behalf of disarmament, Hon. Howard Green, is not here to speak on behalf of the party.
The Prime Minister has pointed out that this is a great forward step. It does not, of course, include underground testing, but even in that regard there are arguments pro and con as to whether the inclusion of underground testing is entirely necessary to assure international and national security. This is the beginning, I hope, of wider negotiations. Certainly the events of the last few weeks have brought about, among all of us in the western world, a hope that we are entering a new era. The signing of this test ban agreement, limited as it is, is a significant step which may presage a new spirit of negotiation.
It has been interesting to follow the statements of Chairman Khrushchev in recent days. About ten days ago he stated that he would permit foreign inspectors to take up stations at Soviet air fields, railway stations, highways and ports to prevent secret concentrations of troops for surprise attack. This offer and his further request for consideration being given to a European non-aggression padt are matters that deserve to be carefully examined. One of the major steps forward yet to be taken toward international disarmament is the control of outer space; agreement among the nations that this infinite area shall not be used for military purposes.
The Prime Minister said in the course of his statement that the present treaty will be
[Mr. Pearson.!

open to all states, and that it is to be hoped there will be the widest possible participation. With that view I entirely concur. I think Canada, because of the closeness of its relationship with France, should be able to do something to bring about an agreement to include France within the purview of this treaty. Certainly the Secretary of State for External Affairs is one who I feel could do a great deal in this connection, to bring about agreement on the part of France through discussions held with General de Gaulle.
Then I think there is a further matter that deserves consideration at this time. That is the question of communist China, a country of 700 million people. By pretending to ignore its existence we do not in fact ignore the tremendous threat that becomes more apparent day by day. Only in the last few days relations between the U.S.S.R. and communist China have indicated a strong division as between those two countries in their thinking. Chairman Khrushchev contends that there is no need to bring about war in order to advance communism; communist China takes the view that revolutionary war is the sole basis for expanding communism. This presents dangerous possibilities. Within a year or two communist China will have nuclear weapons, it is expected.
I think a major challenge is presented to the nations of the western world today. Canada, the United States and other nations will have to take another look at our policy regarding communist China. We will have to review our thinking. We will have to consider the problem, and it is a tremendous one, in the perspective of changing events, and particularly in view of this agreement; because unless it includes communist China-and I do not want to mention France in the same paragraph-and we are able to secure the adherence of communist China, the threat of nuclear war will hang over us to a degree that we can only anticipate with foreboding, horror and overwhelming fear.
I think that the conclusion of this agreement, as the Prime Minister has said, represents what can be achieved by those who are prepared courageously to follow a course of action. Whatever the fears, whatever the setbacks, the word "never" is no longer in the vocabulary of our relations as between east and west; that has been shown by the signing of this test ban. I hope, and I know the house does, that all of us will be able to make our contribution to assure the removal of the threat, which is overshadowing all mankind, of the thermonuclear destruction not only of our country and the free world but of mankind itself.

subsubtopic: NUCLEAR TEST BAN-ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIALLING OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members in this

house join with the Prime Minister in expressing their satisfaction, and the renewed hope for world peace which have been raised in their minds as the result of the announcement which we have just heard and the news which has been coming to us in the last couple of days of the test ban negotiations which have been carried on in Moscow. I am sure that all Canadians, peace loving as we are, look forward with much expectation to this significant step toward bringing about a realization of what we hope for, not only for our country but also for the whole world.
I note with satisfaction, however, that the Prime Minister has been careful to caution us about any degree of overoptimism. Certainly no successful test ban arrangements and no successful disarmament treaty can mean anything unless all aspects are taken care of. While we agree that this is a tremendous step forward and that there is obviously general agreement about the arrangements for a ban on nuclear testing in the three areas which have been mentioned, the fact remains that modern instrumentation has made possible the detection of any such type of testing in any part of the world from any other part of the world. What is being covered now is nothing more nor less than what can be covered by other means as far as the opposing elements of this test ban agreement are concerned.
Therefore, while we do observe this hopeful note, it is imperative that we heed these words of caution, particularly in view of the fact that any agreement of this type must be multilateral; it cannot be unilateral in any of its aspects. I think we all hope within ourselves that this first step might be the beginning of a greater degree of agreement amongst the nations of the world, particularly between the eastern and western elements, toward the objectives of world peace and total disarmament.
I think it is well for us to remember that the problem involved is not just one of nuclear armaments, nor is it just one of general disarmament. The cold war is rapidly taking on new aspects. We must take note of the fact that the Chinese brand of communism and the Soviet brand of communism are at odds with each other. The differences run very deep, perhaps deeper than we realize. Yet there is no evidence that the objective of world communism, whether it is sought through the militaristic attitude of China or through the ideas of co-existence which, apparently, we find in the Soviet union, does not differ in any way. The basic objective in both cases remains the destruction of capitalism and the free way of life which we enjoy in our country, as well as those individual rights which we regard as sacred.

Nuclear Test Ban Agreement
Another aspect of this question which is important is this, and, we are not concerned here with military strength alone. Bound up with the military aspect of this situation are the foreign policies of all the various governments concerned, as well as their economic policies. I am concerned that the economic side of these relationships is rapidly becoming even more important than the military aspect. It has been said that the world is dividing itself into three basic blocs, the communistic states of the east, the free democratic countries of the west and the emerging nations. The attention of each of these groups will be increasingly related to the success of the efforts which are being made to raise economic standards and to improve the standard of living of the individuals composing them. Success in this direction will be the basic element involved if we are to meet the threat posed by communism to our free way of life.
We must, moreover, take careful note that we cannot separate our trade policies, our foreign policies and our defence policies. They must go together. Fragmentation of the over-all picture would merely add to the weakness we have exhibited many times in the past. Thus, while we are pleased with the progress which has been made, we must at all times be cautious to keep the basic issues in correct perspective.
We are grateful to the Prime Minister for bringing this statement to the attention of the house, and we completely agree that Canada should take immediate action to be one of the signatory powers. And if the time should come when there is a break in the wall which tends to divide the people of the world today, we should be there to play our part and do whatever is our responsibility to do.

subsubtopic: NUCLEAR TEST BAN-ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIALLING OF AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the initialling of the test ban agreement by the representatives of the governments of the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet union represents an important milestone in man's march toward peace on earth and the rule of law. Now that the ice jam has been broken it may be possible to move toward greater achievements in establishing peace throughout the world. Undoubtedly the logical next step would be to work for nuclear disarmament among the nuclear powers.
However, before this is possible' the proposal of Premier Khrushchev will have to be considered, namely a non-aggression pact between the NATO nations and the Warsaw pact powers. I hope that Canada as a member of NATO will exercise all its influence toward that end. I think we have reached the stage where we can no longer continue to

House of Commons
posture in rigid, fixed positions. I hope that Canada will use its influence to see that a non-aggression pact between NATO and the Warsaw pact countries is not held up merely in order to preserve the myth that East Germany does not exist.
I was glad to hear the Prime Minister say that Canada would subscribe to this agreement. I hope, however, that we will do much more. At the present time the warm winds of understanding and tolerance are beginning to blow across the cold war. This is the time for nations to take the initiative and to remove the clouds of suspicion that have covered the eyes of the nations. Canada could do much by taking the initiative in this regard.
I think Canada ought to reconsider its position with reference to the recognition of red China and the admission of red China into the United Nations provided, of course, she is prepared to become a law abiding member of the world community. As I have said repeatedly in the house, I think this is an excellent opportunity for the Canadian government to say that in the interests of stopping the spread of nuclear arms in the world, Canada is prepared to reconsider its position with reference to the acquisition of nuclear arms. I am sure that if in the course of the next few days or weeks the Prime Minister was prepared to make an announcement that Canada was reconsidering its position in the light of the improved international situation and was prepared as its contribution to forgo the acquisition of nuclear arms, this would do much toward promoting the kind of understanding and good will which are basically essential to any further progress on the road to peace.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):

Mr. Speaker, I have a statement to make on government organization and one to make on house business. Perhaps I may be permitted to combine them. The first one is very short. I wish to announce that The Department of Industry Act was proclaimed yesterday, that Hon. C. M. Drury, Minister of Defence Production, was sworn in today as Minister of Industry and that David A. Golden is to be deputy minister.
Ministerial responsibility for the department of public printing and stationery was transferred today from the Secretary of State to the Minister of Industry in accordance with a recommendation of the Glassco commission report and, I may add, with the approval of the Secretary of State.
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition asked me about the general plan of the government for the remainder of this portion

of the session, and also asked when the government expected that parliament would reconvene. I undertook to make a statement today, and I now propose to do so. The house leader, the Secretary of State, has been in regular consultation with representatives of the parties opposite in arranging the business of the house and has, I understand, given them a general indication of what the government hopes to accomplish before we adjourn for what is left of the summer. I believe I can summarize this very briefly.
Today we are going on with the one remaining budget resolution, to be followed by the excise tax bill. The government also wishes to complete consideration of the bill respecting the surcharge order and the committee stage and third reading of the bill respecting the economic council. As for the municipal development and loan board bill and the resolution respecting the Canada pension plan, these, as hon. members know, are to be the subject of consultation with the premiers of the provinces tomorrow and Saturday. I believe it will be a courtesy to the provinces to reserve any statement regarding the government's plans with respect to these two matters until Monday, when a statement can be made in the light of this conference.
The government will also ask for interim supply for the months of August and September. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, we plan to bring in a supplementary estimate which will be largely concerned with the maintenance of employment, and which it would be the hope of the government that the committee of supply would adopt so that this item could be included in the interim supply bill. The government has not yet completed its consideration of the Norris report, and it is possible that we may be in a position next week to ask the house to consider a measure arising out of the recommendations of that report.
I know of no other business that the government feels it should be necessary to have completed before the adjournment, except for two items which we would like the house to be able to deal with in this part of the session. Subject to further consultation between the house leader and hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to procedure, the government is ready to take the responsibility tomorrow of proposing certain changes in the remuneration and pensions of members of parliament, and we would like at the same time to deal with certain amendments to the Judges Act which, in the opinion of the government, should be made before the adjournment if possible.

It would be the hope of the government that with the co-operation of all hon. members we might complete the business of this part of the session by the middle or latter part of next week, and in that case it might be possible to adjourn until Monday, September 30.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Prime Minister for his outline. While I am in entire agreement with the date fixed for adjournment, if the program to which he has referred is to receive the proper attention that parliament must give to it then it would seem that, as has happened so often in the past, prime ministers are often too optimistic in setting dates for the termination of sessions.
In so far as the house business is concerned, I feel that any action to be taken should be in accordance with the usual method and should follow the rules. There was a suggestion that tomorrow, provided there was consent, certain matters could be proceeded with. Now that we are in the middle of the budget discussion I believe we should continue with that and that the government in the regular course should place on the order paper whatever motion it desires to place thereon. Certainly there will be no great delay.
I am sure we would be subject to a great deal of criticism if the house were to decide by agreement that the rules are to be set aside in respect of a matter particularly affecting the house. People across the country would say "You delay other matters because of the necessity of compliance with the rules, but on matters affecting each and every member of the house and the Senate you have no qualms in asking for consent consideration immediately". In my view a motion could be made returnable on Monday in the regular course of events, in which case that argument could not be used because the regular processes of parliament would have been followed.
I suggest to the Prime Minister in all sincerity that the course suggested by him could only lead to people believing that when we deal with matters affecting ourselves the rules are brushed aside. One extra day's consideration through a motion being properly placed before the house will meet any such general criticism.

speechtext: Can the Minister of Finance inform the house whether, in the course of the discussion on finance which took place in Washington during the week end, the possibility of unpegging the Canadian dollar was raised?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: INQUIRIES RESPECTING U.S. MODIFICATION OF TAX IMPOSED
speechtext:
I shall be delighted to answer that question, but I should like to place the answer in the proper context.
In the week end discussions in Washington there was a full and frank discussion between Canadian and United States representatives of all aspects of the payments position of the two countries. This naturally included a discussion of the capital movements between the two countries and of the various factors affecting them. As members of the house are aware, one of these factors-by no means the only one, but an important one-is the relative level of interest rates in the two countries.
The Canadian representatives explained, as I had informed the house on the evening of June 13, that the monetary policy of the government and, of course, of the Bank of Canada was directed to achieving the kind of credit conditions which would favour economic expansion in Canada while keeping the needs of the balance of payments situation in mind. They pointed out that there had been a progressive reduction for some time in the level of interest rates in Canada and in the spread between interest rates in Canada and the United States, and said that in the present economic circumstances of large unemployment and substantial unutilized capacity it would continue to be the aim of Canadian policy to encourage credit conditions which were at once stimulating to the Canadian economy and compatible with exchange stability and balance in our international accounts.
The United States representatives were naturally interested primarily in the effects of the policies followed on their short term liabilities to Canada in the form of Canada's holdings of United States dollars which together with our gold holdings, constitute our exchange reserves. The Canadian representatives pointed out that during the latter part of 1962 it had been necessary to encourage a volume of borrowing abroad sufficient not only to cover our current account but also build up our depleted exchange reserves, and that this had led temporarily to abnormally large borrowings in the United States; that once the reserves had been rebuilt to more satisfactory levels, the policy had been, in the prevailing circumstances, to achieve a capital inflow no more than sufficient to cover the reduced current account deficit, and the success of this policy was reflected in the fact
Inquiries of the Ministry that during the first half of 1963 Canada's exchange reserves had remained very stable if one excludes the receipt in January, 1963, of the second half of the $250 million United States loan arranged in September, 1962. The Canadian representatives were accordingly authorized to provide the assurance, which is reflected in the communique, that it was not the desire or intention of Canada to take advantage of unlimited exemption from the proposed United States tax to increase her foreign exchange reserves through the proceeds of borrowing in the United States. This has, in any case, not been recent Canadian policy.
Exemption from the United States tax will undoubtedly enable Canada to maintain a lower level of interest rates than would have been possible if the tax were applied to us, and the general level of interest rates in Canada will be lower than it would have to be if we were aiming at increasing our exchange reserves by encouraging a volume of borrowing which, when taken in conjunction with the net of all other capital movements, was more than sufficient to cover our current account deficit. But members will, I am sure, realize that no one can forecast with certainty what the precise level of interest rates in Canada will be, since this depends on a variety of factors which cannot now be foreseen, including the trend of interest rates in the United States and elsewhere. Consequently it would not have been possible for any undertaking to have been given regarding the future of interest rates in Canada.
Now, to answer the hon. member's question about the exchange rate, there has been some question as to whether the possibility of Canada abandoning the fixed rate of the Canadian dollar was raised in the Washington discussions. The answer is in the negative. I have stated in the house that it is the policy of the government to maintain and defend the fixed exchange rate for the Canadian dollar at its present level, and this policy was not called into question by United States representatives in the Washington discussions. The last sentence of the communique issued after the talks records that active discussions will continue to strengthen the close economic relations between the two countries and, at the same time, facilitate measures for making the maximum practicable contributions to economic expansion in both countries and the strength and stability of both currencies.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be appropriate for a minister of this government to comment on revelations, shocking though they may be, made before a committee of another legislative body.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Has the minister received a letter of resignation from the acting assistant deputy minister, Dr. Kristjansson?

speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. speechtext:

speechtext:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, could I ask the Secretary of State how soon he expects to get a report from the three gentlemen in question.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Forestry. Would the minister advise the house if any progress is being made in discussions with the government of Nova Scotia related to the forest stand improvement program in the Cape Breton area of that province?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Forestry):
subsubtopic: PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to inform the house that the government has approved the extension for another year of the agreement with the province of Nova Scotia covering the forest stand improvement program for Cape Breton. subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADA'S CONTRIBUTION TO WORLD FOOD PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in relation to the statement made yesterday concerning Canada's increased contribution to the world food program. Has he consulted with Dr. Sem, director general of F.A.O., or Dr. Burmah, director of the world food program, in relation to this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADA'S CONTRIBUTION TO WORLD FOOD PROGRAM
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I personally did not have any talks with them on this particular subject. The officials of the government are, of course, in constant touch with the officials of the food and agriculture organization.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADA'S CONTRIBUTION TO WORLD FOOD PROGRAM
speechtext: A supplementary question. Would the minister give an assurance to the house that the commitment as to the ratio between food and cash assistance by the previous minister of agriculture will be maintained?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADA'S CONTRIBUTION TO WORLD FOOD PROGRAM

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADA'S CONTRIBUTION TO WORLD FOOD PROGRAM
speechtext: A further supplementary question. Were there consultations between President Kennedy or Secretary of Agriculture Orville Freeman with regard to the impact of Canada's enlargement of giveaway programs, and their pledge not to extend United States giveaway programs following the vote on the referendum which was held in the United States?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADA'S CONTRIBUTION TO WORLD FOOD PROGRAM
speechtext: No. As I said yesterday our program of expanded aid, which will take the form of further shipments of wheat and flour to needy countries, will be expanded in consultation with other countries, including the United States, and it will be done in such a way as to give ample protection to the markets of those countries as well as ours.
On the orders of the day:

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED NON-AGGRESSION PACT WITH WARSAW PACT COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In the light of the encouraging and momentous statement made today by the Prime Minister, is it the intention of the government to express to its allies in NATO the belief that a non-aggression treaty between NATO and

the Warsaw pact powers might make a useful contribution to the easing of tensions between these two blocs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED NON-AGGRESSION PACT WITH WARSAW PACT COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the conference to which the Prime Minister directed our attention earlier today has concluded. The negotiators are returning to their respective governments. In the communique which has been issued, they have indicated that they will report afterwards to the members of the NATO council, and the Soviet union will report to the members of the Warsaw pact.
When those reports take place Canada will be fully informed. The government has already indicated that subject to obligations and positions taken with regard to the problem of a divided Germany, we see advantage, all things considered, in a reaffirmation by the nations that they will not commit aggression. Before a final position can be taken, my hon. friend will understand that we will have to await the report to the NATO council and the attitude taken by other member states of NATO.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED NON-AGGRESSION PACT WITH WARSAW PACT COUNTRIES
speechtext: supplementary question. Might I ask the minister what commitments Canada has with reference to a divided Germany?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED NON-AGGRESSION PACT WITH WARSAW PACT COUNTRIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Canada has no commitments. Canada has stated her views in this house, as it did through the previous government. We will have to give these views consideration before a final position can be taken. I would not want what I have said to be interpreted as meaning that it would not be possible to make a declaration on the part of members of NATO and members of the Warsaw pact which would take into account the considerations I mentioned a moment ago.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a supplementary question. subtopic: REPORTED REFUSAL TO PERMIT RE-ENLISTMENT OF PETTY OFFICER
speechtext:
Some time ago the hon. member for Winnipeg North asked if I had received a report of the review of the circumstances relating to the termination of Mr. Eric Petersen's service in the Royal Canadian Navy. As the hon. member knows, the occurrence took place in 1961, but I can now give the house the following information.
Non-commissioned officers and men enlist for a fixed period of years, and when that period expires it is at the option of the
[Mr. Deschatelets.l

service involved and of the man whether reengagement is offered or accepted. In the case of Mr. Petersen, re-engagement was not offered and he was given an honourable discharge without any qualifications that might prejudice either his future employment elsewhere or his standing in whatever community in which he might choose to reside. Having looked into the matter thoroughly, I do not intend to alter the decision taken by the Royal Canadian Navy at that time.

removal of the Minister of Finance, because I do not know what we would do if we did not have him to blame for the mistakes that are being made for the government. He is not responsible directly for many of them, but he is now the involuntary recipient of criticism in every part of Canada.
What is our stand? Number one, we say the budget should be withdrawn. We realize that the government having backed up, receded and retreated will not be able to go that far. They will not be able to do that. But I still think they should give consideration, if they want the economy of Canada to expand, to the withdrawing of this tax on building materials and production machinery. If they do not do so, the events of the last few weeks indicate that a body blow was struck by the budget to economic expansion, the purpose for which the budget was established.
In so far as this budget is concerned, the longer it is being considered the more it is being criticized. It is a self emasculating instrument, detrimental to the Canadian economy. The purpose was to build, and the effect is to diminish. I ask, Mr. Chairman, who, in a desire to expand capital investment, ever taxed the investment itself? I am not going to go back on that in detail. This tax against capital investment is wrong in principle. The fact that it was wrong in principle was shown by the retreat. Does it become right because it is being applied in instalments?
Surely the statistics of the last few weeks should cause this government, even now, to stop to consider. They cannot hurt their reputation for retreats. It is impossible to do that. This would be an act of courage, for there is no courage in stubbornly adhering to a policy which in every part of Canada is recognized as deleterious to the expansion of our country. The sales tax, under the instalment plan, is not as severe at it was originally. However, the graduation of the tax compounds its inequality, to use an expression of the financial critic of the Montreal Gazette. It is a tax on jobs in every part of Canada.
What has been the effect on industry? In the month of June there was a falling off in building contract awards of almost 20 per cent, according to the statistics that are available. The government says it wants to make industry competitive in a world in which the challenge from other parts of the world becomes greater and greater. Do you make industry competitive by adding an extra cost on industry by taxation on machinery of about $100 million? The position of the opposition-and I summarize since I am not going into detail because the subject has been covered in detail by various members who have spoken-is that the objective is denied

by the imposition of this tax. They used to speak about how bad things were in Canada. They shouted "Get the economy rolling." They have now got it on the way downhill; that is the easiest direction.
I repeat only in one particular what I said the other day. When we had an addition of 8 per cent to the gross national product last year, they said the economy should be set rolling. They spoke about indecision and inaction, but this year they predict an increase of only 5 per cent. They said we should expand construction expenditures across Canada. Last year they increased 5.2 per cent, but before the tax was imposed the estimate for this year was reduced to 4.5 per cent.
They said business capital expansion would be right around the corner if they got into office. It was 7 per cent last year, and according to the estimate it will be 5.5 per cent this year. They said "Let us expand exports." We found markets for our exports, but they said we were not expanding fast enough. The increase in exports last year was 7.8 per cent over the previous year, but this year the estimate is that it will be 5 per cent.
There were some corporations in the larger cities across Canada who said they could not give us support because they were not doing as well as they should. However, their corporation profits last year amounted to 11 per cent. This year the estimate is 6 per cent to 7 per cent, not because prices have gone up or down, but simply because of the fact that the economy is not rolling except in the one direction. That is why we ask the government to give leadership in this regard. That is why we suggest action be taken now before it is too late. It is all very well to have an objective, but when you see the objective is not being met it is the height of dangerous obstinacy to follow a course which the experience of only a few weeks has shown to be wrong.
When I take that stand, Mr. Chairman, remember that is the stand this party took from the beginning. On the night the budget was introduced I issued a statement and said it was a retrogressive budget and would interfere with expansion. When it came to a vote, the Conservative party voted solidly against the budget. They did not have any uncertainty about it; they knew it was bad. The Social Credit party talked eloquently against it but then swallowed their beliefs by voting for the budget which they now criticize.
Let's be honest, John.
Let me say to my hon. friends that their conduct in the last few weeks has shown they have become a dilapidated annex of the Liberal party.
Rubbish.
I know it is difficult. I know how you feel because you did not vote as you said.
Oh, oh.
Oh, yes, you did. If they voted as they said, then I do not understand the kind of arithmetic that causes a party to say it does not believe in these things and then vote for them. That is beyond me.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, is there not a rule about reflecting on votes of the house, a rule of the house that the right hon. gentleman in his passion seems to have transgressed?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sure that the right hon. Leader of the Opposition realizes the importance of abiding by that rule.

I was not commenting on a vote of the house in a way that transgresses the rule. So far as the hon. gentleman opposite is concerned, he is up all the time. The first time you are here you are impressed, as the cuckoo is heard in June but not regarded in July. Why is there this tremendous interest on his part in bringing before the house the impossible position in which the Social Credit party is? So far as the N.D.P. are concerned, they have strong views. They did not vote at all.
We voted with you last year.
I can only let them explain the reason for that peculiar, unusual and rather unexpected course.
We did not agree with you, but we voted with you last year.

The hon. gentleman says "We did not agree with you last year but we supported you." Does not that indicate a concept regarding the serious responsibility of individual members of parliament? I am glad to have that admission, and I welcome any further interruptions of the kind.
You liked it last year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I suggest that we should have order in the committee.

I could not better like interruptions such as the hon. gentleman's contributions. I welcome them at any time, because he lets the cat out of the bag. He is just showing how consistent they are. Last year they did not like us and they voted for us; this year they did not like the budget and they voted for it. How can anyone call that inconsistency?
To return to my speech after this interesting interlude, I want to ask the government what is being done in connection
Excise Tax Act
with the very important matter of those refunds. On July 9 the Minister of National Revenue said:
When refunds are made to the manufacturers, importers or others who have remitted the tax to the department, or where they have made deductions from the tax they would have had to pay and thus achieved the same result, it will, of course, be expected that they will pass on these benefits to those to whom they sold goods during this period.
It is natural that when one is in public life, one gets letters criticizing things, and businessmen across Canada are asking what is going to be done about this. It is the government that made the mistake. It imposed an 11 per cent tax and told business people, "Start collecting it tonight." The people of Canada relied on the government. The 11 per cent tax was collected, but what attitude did the government take then? As reported at page 1974 of Hansard of July 9, the hon. member for Wellington South asked this question:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct my question to the Minister of National Revenue following the announcement just made by the Minister of Finance. Would the Minister of National Revenue advise the house as to the procedure an individual would follow to obtain a refund in excess of the 4 per cent rate, as announced last night?

Hire a lawyer.
The advice is good. You and I could not disagree with that, Mr. Chairman, but that is not very fair to the person who has been taken as a result of the changed attitude on the part of the government. Then the Minister of National Revenue said:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member who has asked the question will appreciate that as a federal government we cannot enter into the relationship between the vendor and the purchaser, but I did rather anticipate that a question along this line might be asked today and I would be happy to tell him this, if I have permission.
I had better read it all, because I do not want to delete any part of it. The minister went on to say:
Last evening the Minister of Finance indicated that refunds would be made to those who during the period from June 14 to July 9 have actually remitted sales tax at the full rate on goods they had sold or imported that were previously exempt. When refunds are made to the manufacturers, importers or others who have remitted the tax to the department, or where they have made deductions from the tax they would have had to pay and thus achieved the same result, it will, of course, be expected that they will pass on these benefits to those to whom they sold goods during this period. In fact it is expected that these benefits will be passed along to the final purchaser. The extent to which this will happen will depend to a considerable degree on the legal and even the good will relations between the vendor and the purchaser.

That is quite inexcusable. There is no cooperation at all in that. They say, "You should be getting it". What happens to the man who bought lumber from the lumber yard in those days?
Mr. Chairman, could I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.
To what part of my reply does he object?
You pulled a boner.

I object to the utter effrontery of saying to the people of Canada who paid 11 per cent, "Try and get it back in the best way you can. We will not give you any assistance whatever, because this is a vendor and purchaser relationship, with which we cannot become involved". That is what I say. I know the difficulties, but I know how reasonable the minister is at all times and I ask him to see whether he cannot bring about some plan of regulations which will enable the original purchaser, the intermediary and finally the retailer, to receive the amount of the rebate, for unless there is assistance on the part of the federal government millions of dollars are going to be in the hands of those who collected them and there will be no place to hand them back.

Mr. Chairman, I know the former prime minister wants to be fair in this. Does he not fully appreciate the fact that the tax collected for the dates he has referred to is not even due until the end of this month?

Oh, now; it was collected day by day after the 13th day of June in every part of this country. They were directed to do so. I say, what is going to be done on the part of the federal government to help the various levels of purchasers to recover the amount of, I do not know how many millions but it certainly must be $7 million or $8 million on the basis of there being a reasonable degree of equality of purchase throughout the year.
I impress upon the minister to come down from that throne on which he seated himself in those remarks in the house and do something to bring about a fair degree of distribution of the excess that was extorted from the Canadian people, not because of any wrongdoing on the part of any of the wholesalers or the retailers but because of the ineptitude of this government, which acted before it thought.
Hear, hear.
The hon. gentleman says, "Why, we do not have to worry about that until the end of this month". Let me read to him the representations of the Canadian construction association.
Mr. Chairman, as the Leader of the Opposition must know, I did not say that at all.
Well, Mr. Chairman, if I misunderstood the hon. gentleman, I would like to know what he did say. I give him an opportunity of clarification.

I will be delighted to explain it again. I said that the tax collected to which the right hon. gentleman is referring and which he says many of his fellow Canadians are misusing and making a windfall of-he has said this on other occasions also-actually is not payable by the parties concerned, to the federal government, until the end of this month.

Mr. Chairman, I say at once that I never did say they were going to be crooked about it. I said there was no assistance on the part of the federal government to arrange for the compensation in the appropriate manner of those who paid that tax; who because of the change that took place now find themselves having overpaid a matter of 7 per cent. Let that be clear.

Let me read what the Canadian construction association says. This brief was written on July 18 and is headed, "Re: Revised budget resolutions". This has not anything to do with the original resolutions; this applies to the revised version. We are wondering whether it is going to be the authorized one too; whether it is going to be final. The Canadian construction association says:
Whereas the imposition of the tax by stages announced by you on July 8 ... a most welcome development, the fact remains that the Department of National Revenue has been unable to issue sufficient rulings as to the application or administration of the 4 per cent sales tax or to establish practicable refund procedures so that the construction industry has any degree of firm guidance on current projects or those now out to tender.
In other words, the Department of National Revenue, the minister, has failed; that is what they say. He joins the Minister of Finance in the failure. He just brings up the rear, as it were; he takes whatever is left over. But the fact remains that it is he who is criticized. Then it says:
This is not meant to be an adverse criticism of federal taxation officials; they are literally so swamped with questions and requests for rulings and the problems of setting up the new procedures that the new sales tax policy necessitates that it will inevitably be months before the present turmoil, confusion and inability to get decisions being experienced within our industry can reasonably be expected to be overcome.
Listen to these words. I could not possibly equal the strength of the attack of the construction industry in these words, "confusion, turmoil, inability to get decisions". These be

the magic workers who, a few short months ago, told us to just sit there and watch things go. Then it goes on:
These words-
They are the words "turmoil, confusion and inability to get decisions being experienced within our industries"-
-describing conditions in the industry were not selected lightly. A good many tender calls and contract awards are being held up.
What I rise to ask for, in connection with that, is that the government let us know what is going to be done. Let them raise the curtain of secrecy in connection with the regulations. What has been done towards drafting them? What are the general conditions to be followed? I made it perfectly clear when I raised the matter in question form some weeks ago, that there was leadership needed on the part of the government to protect Canadians from the mistakes of the government, from its lack of decision, from its vacillating stands, and from the regular alteration of various sections of the budget.
I go on, Mr. Chairman, to deal with the lumber industry. I mention the lumber industry because it has been seriously affected, and I refer to the Canadian Weekly highlights in which the following appeared with regard to British Columbia. It deals first of all with the expansion of foreign trade and says:
Total foreign trade in the first five months of 1963 reached a new high of $5.1 billion. These results are very encouraging and the Canadian dollar discount has been a most favourable factor. Further improvement appears in prospect over the balance of the year.
Lumber shipments: British Columbia saw mills
shipped 1,968 million board foot of lumber in the first four months of 1963, an increase of 7.1 per cent over ... the like 1962 period ...
The gain to date is impressive but is not expected to continue at this rate in view of the new tax on building materials, recently reduced from 11 per cent to 4 per cent.
That is British Columbia.
With regard to the maritimes, the maritime lumber bureau said this as of July 17:
Marketing of lumber, in comparison to other materials, is recognized as a highly specialized operation. Because of its versatility in use, it is marketed in different sizes-
And so on. And it goes on to say this:
In the Atlantic provinces, particularly, there are a thousand saw mills alone, besides dressing mills and woodworking shops in almost every village.
As the tax is set up, with all its complicated applications and exemptions at each level of lumber's manufacture and processing, it becomes quite evident to the lumber industry that it is impracticable and unworkable-
That is the considered opinion of the maritime lumber bureau, a completely non-partisan body, and it must soon be apparent to

the department that net returns to the government will not warrant the expense of administration. This report goes on:
We believe that lumber associations across Canada will have to continue to move against this tax for sheer survival.
That is how serious is the situation, but the only answer I get from the other side of the chamber is jeers when I suggest that even yet the sales tax on building materials should not only be abrogated but abolished. The report concludes:
Certainly the maritime lumber bureau in the interests of the Atlantic provinces must continue the battle until this most injurious and unacceptable load on the industry is removed.

Mr. Speaker, last week when it was brought before the house, we heard this bill being opposed by some hon. members, including the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire).

The latter raised several objections which, I feel, should be questioned if we are to entertain good relations with the various countries which do business with Canada.
Surely, we are obliged to accept the fact that foreign capital, especially from the United States, should further Canada's economic development. It is to be regretted that the Social Credit doctrine is not yet in force, for that is why we have to use foreign capital if the affairs of our country are to run smoothly. However, the fact should have been emphasized, during the discussion of this bill, that Canadians should adopt a positive attitude, not a negative one, as regards those who wish to settle here in Canada. Canadians themselves should be proud to be Canadians and should encourage Canadian companies to make their investments work for Canada and not for foreign countries.
In my opinion, it is unthinkable that Canadians should adopt legislation to prevent other companies from settling in Canada, especially when we know very well that a foreign company can sell insurance in Canada without being incorporated. Of course, that makes things harder, but nothing prevents Canadian citizens from taking insurance policies with American companies, even if they do not have offices in Canada. That Simp-sons-Sears is affiliated with Sears-Roebuck, that it is to a large extent controlled by American citizens, those are facts that we must deplore as Canadians but, in my opinion, companies that have decided to invest in our country should not be penalized.
Counter insurance sale was mentioned. Well, that is an economical way to sell insurance and nothing prevents Canadians from doing the same.
Instead of always approaching the problem in a negative way, again I am of the opinion that we should stimulate the pride of the Canadian citizen and urge him to buy his insurance at home, from a Canadian company, which will enable him at the same time to invest in his own country.
The hon. member for Lapointe said last Thursday that insurance companies represent one of the largest pools of savings that can be used for the economic development of a nation. That is true and I think that the legislation could perhaps favour a little more the economic development of Canada if, for instance, the government decided to re-

Private Bills
quire of foreign companies that profits made in Canada should be re-invested in our country, in Canadian industries. That would be a much more positive action, more in favour of Canada than action directed against foreign countries or against foreigners who wish to invest in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, that is why I feel that we cannot oppose the passage of this legislation.
But since we are on second reading, we can express our views about the principle governing all those American corporations who come to do business in Canada.
And what is most amazing is the fact that one day we are complaining that there is too much American capital in Canada and the next we complain that the U.S. government wants to prevent American citizens from investing in our country. Therefore we are wondering whether we are not actually simply arguing negatively against all and any motion introduced. Despite all our qualms about incorporating the Allstate Company in Canada, I believe that in all fairness and sincerity, it is most difficult to oppose the measure, since the corporation must follow rules established by the Canadian government.
However, I hope that the Canadian government will in the future accept its responsibilities and insert both in the insurance companies act and the act regarding companies intending to invest in Canada a clause to prevent the management of foreign corporations investing in Canada to return home with the profits they have made on the premiums and interests paid by Canadian citizens.
Mr. Speaker, those were the few remarks that I wanted to make, even though several parts of the speech of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) could be taken up. Besides, I feel that we should always take positive action so as to favour Canadian citizens, instead of taking a negative position which would prevent people from other countries from investing money in Canada, especially when we realize that they have to comply with the regulations established by the Canadian government.

There is some argument for using United States capital to develop our natural resources, because there are some side or beneficial effects to that sort of development. But this United States company will simply duplicate services that are presently provided to better advantage by numerous other companies in Canada.
This is simply to provide the opportunity to mobilize Canadian savings to the advantage of the company. There is a very big difference between an insurance company and a company interested in production.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad that at last I am able to take up the caveat I registered last night on some time in the debate today, and I hope to continue the address which was received with such great approval on both sides of the house last night. I hope that when I have finished my address it will receive the same approval, but I doubt it. It was a pleasure to give up my allotted time this afternoon to the leader of my party. It is a very difficult thing to follow perhaps the most able debater in Canada and what I will have to say will probably be somewhat of an anticlimax to his speech. However, I feel that at this time I should say something about the resolution, and particularly the budget.

I was, I must say, more than surprised by the budget when it was presented by the Minister of Finance. What surprises me more than anything is the stony silence that has prevailed throughout on the part of the front-bench members of the government. Not one of the old pros in the government has risen to speak on behalf of the Minister of Finance, although he has been found fault with and criticized by almost everybody in Canada.
The minister says that he has some telegrams and letters commending him for his budget, but that is not the kind of letters and telegrams I have received. The 11 per cent tax on building materials and industrial machinery has been watered down a bit, of course, but I presume that in the course of time it will reach the full 11 per cent again. The fact that the tax has been criticized by almost everybody in Canada and that it has caused so much unemployment that was not in evidence before, and for which there was really no reason, is very bad advertising for the new government, the Minister of Finance and, of course for Canada.
So far as the 30 per cent withholding tax is concerned, the minister withdrew that very quickly on the request of a few of his millionaire friends and it certainly did not take him very long to do that. However, it took over a month and perhaps half a million requests from people all over Canada to get him to change the effect of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, even to the extent that he has.
It is a very bad thing when everybody in Canada complains about a budget. It may be it was a good thing to impose a tax that affects almost everybody, but it is also a very bad thing in that it taxes one of the activities that the government was hoping would cause more employment in Canada and a great deal more activity. The fact is that in the result it has not helped to relieve unemployment at all.
Another thing I am very surprised at is that the revaluation of the dollar to 92J cents in relation to United States currency during the Conservative regime was left alone, in spite of all the complaints and criticisms that the Liberal party and the Minister of Finance himself, notwithstanding his attitude in his book, "Troubled Canada", had levelled at the former government. They complained about it and said it would ruin Canada's economy.
I trust you are not going to stop me talking about that, Mr. Chairman. That is one of the very bad results of the budget and of these taxes. I noticed you were getting to your feet, Mr. Chairman. I presume you do not like me talking about the whole budget, but everybody else has been doing so, so I do not see how you can stop me.

A budget is supposed to be the brainchild of the Minister of Finance and perhaps the Prime Minister, in any event, of the government. When this budget was brought in it was not the brainchild of the government. It was brought in by the Minister of Finance, but apparently neither the Prime Minister nor any of the other ministers had ever heard of it before it was presented, because members on this side could see the look of dismay on their faces. It was something to behold, believe me.
The Minister of Finance has admitted, and it has been proven, that the budget was prepared by four assistants who were not members of the civil service. This, in itself, is an insult to the civil service, which has given such great service to Canada, and especially to the deputy minister of finance who has since left the department. He may have been given a promotion or he may not. It may have been at his own request; who knows? In any event, this budget that was presented was definitely not a budget that represented the feelings of the government. If the Minister of Finance has to consult other people, he could have consulted some 90 members of the Liberal party who occupy the back benches. He would have obtained a great deal better advice than he did from the members of financial houses in Toronto. He would have had a budget that was representative and approved by the people of Canada. This is one of the things he has learned, and believe me there are a lot of other things he must learn.
Of course, I have referred to this budget as the illegitimate brainchild of the four members of the financial houses in Toronto, and it has occurred to me that perhaps we should now question also the parentage of the minister's book "Troubled Canada". Canada really now has more cause to be troubled than she ever did before because the Minister of Finance has not realized he was supposed to present a budget that would be acceptable to the people of Canada and that would really help the economy of this country. It seems that now we have a government by Gordon, ghostwriters and gimmicks instead of, as in former times, government by crystal ball.
As I have remarked before, all the fault does not lie with the minister. Some of it must lie with the other members on the front benchers, because they allowed the minister to bring down a budget like that and, therefore, they could not have known what was in it. This must be one of the things that is worrying them now because not one of them has stood up to defend the Minister of Finance. This is something about which the people of Canada are wondering. Of course, the Secretary of State has given the minister answers when he has been asked questions, but he has not got up to speak in defence
Excise Tax Act
of the Minister of Finance. Of course, you could not expect anything else. The old pros in the front ranks of the cabinet are the same old pros as were there in 1957 when the government was thrown out of office by the people of Canada. There are two missing. The former prime minister is not here to hold them together, and neither is that man who was the government of Canada. He has gone to his great reward. I am referring to the late Hon. C. D. Howe. He was, at that time, the government of Canada and he ruled the roost. There was not any question about that.
I do not propose to take much more of the time of the committee. However, I am wondering how in the name of heaven the Minister of Finance proposes to legislate the people of Canada into investing their money in Canada. The trend seems to be that people who have money to invest invest it in places outside of Canada. They do not support industries in Canada. Whenever an industry in Canada is for sale, it is the people from outside the country who buy it. One has only to look at the case of Cockshutt Plow Company, which was the only Canadian implement company left, to find they sold out to foreign buyers.
If today the Canadian National Railways were put up for sale you would not find a buyer anywhere that would pay a proper price for it. However, if the Polymer Corporation, which is another child of the government, were put up for sale you would find plenty of buyers from all over the world. I do not know whether you would find any people from Canada willing to buy it, but it is a going concern. It pays its way. Why is it that Canadian businessmen who have money to invest, will invest in stocks or shares from other countries rather than invest their money in Canada? Perhaps the shares pay a quarter of 1 per cent more interest or dividend. This is something that I have never been able to understand. Why do people in Canada who have money to invest not invest that money in Canada?
I suggest also to the minister that if he wanted to impose a new tax that would be quite unpopular, but which is really a tax that should be in effect, he should investigate the possibility of taxing capital gains. I know that would meet the approval of my friends to the far left, but it might not meet with the approval of too many people who have money to invest in Canada. This is a place where a tax could be imposed that would be a fair tax.
Now, having made these few remarks, I shall conclude. I do not intend to lengthen this debate and I do not want to be accused of delaying this measure.

It still remains a mystery to most Canadians why the exemptions applied to building materials should be withdrawn at this particular time. The fact that the building and allied trades constitute one of our best means of creating employment makes it even more mystifying. The reduction from 11 per cent to 4 per cent- a concession, I might say, that was wrung from the minister-while cushioning the immediate impact of the full tax on construction does not alter the fact that a good many people in this country who had intended to build or renovate property are having second thoughts in this regard.
The minister's explanation that this particular tax was necessary to help reduce the budget deficit, it seems to me, is certainly shortsighted, because a reduction in the construction program across the country will reduce, rather than add to, the taxes forthcoming from this particular industry. Surely there were other means of finding revenue that would not adversely affect employment and private and industrial development as much as this one. In addition the construction industry lost three vital weeks during the debacle that followed the introduction of the budget-a budget, I might say, that ran counter to the government's boast that they would increase employment and get the economy rolling. The removal of the tax exemption on building materials on an escalating scale starting at 4 per cent certainly does not give any encouragement for expansion in that industry.
The gimmick type of approach used in the budget leads one to believe that it was written up or put together by a group of inept merchandisers rather than fiscal experts. A case in point is the $500 prize offered for winter construction, a measure that has been rather effectively erased by the imposition of the tax on building materials. The gimmick approach seems to have set the theme for the whole affair and has now become the symbol of the Liberal party-gimmicks born of ineptitude out of expediency. The three opposition parties stated their opposition to the 11 per cent sales tax, but each in its own way.

But I think we must also keep in mind that many Canadians voted for members of the present government on the promises, even commitments, of its candidates to get the economy going, to increase employment and to balance the budget. I will not go any further into other promises or what the people expected of the party which formed the government. Perhaps people are now beginning to realize that they bought the Brooklyn bridge. In the first place, this government will finish out its fiscal year with the biggest deficit in the history of this country. My prediction is that because of the methods being used there will be more unemployment, and this budget has already gone down in history as the worst one ever brought in since confederation. To substantiate this, if it needs any substantiation, one needs only to read from a little booklet published by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association called "Industry". This article is entitled "Opportunity lost", and says:
From the manufacturing standpoint,-
Is there a doctor in the house?

They need several:
-however, the most dismaying and least forgivable feature of the budget is the extension of the 11 per cent sales tax to machinery and apparatus-
This, of course, was before it was reduced to 4 per cent:
-and processing materials used in the production of goods, and to building materials used in the construction of new factories and plant extensions.
Manufacturers already are required to pay the sales tax on the goods they produce; they are now to be made to pay it on the machinery used in the production of these same goods. In effect, they

will be paying the tax twice over. This isn't just; it isn't wise; and it certainly isn't expansionist.
The likely corporate reaction is all too predictable. In reviewing, as they will be bound to do, their capital spending intentions, some companies will reluctantly decide to defer the purchase of needed plant and equipment and to "make do" for a while longer. Still others with plans for expanding their capacity or building plants may well decide that the higher outlay compels them to hold off for now.
