"Regressive and regrettable" was the budget night comment of H. Roy Crabtree, president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association-
In my humble opinion the Minister of Finance would not be in the difficulties in which he now finds himself had he used the wisdom and experience of his own department. Surely there are few people with as much experience as the people in the finance department, who have years of experience behind them in preparing budgets. They are in possession of a wealth of experience and have unquestionably studied the economy at length. They would have charted a much safer course for the Minister of Finance. Instead he was led down the garden path into the briar patch by a group of amateurs. This is, of course, what one could really call the second budget because in this resolution the tax on building materials has been reduced from 11 per cent to 4 per cent. However, this is just not good enough; it should be eliminated completely for at least a year, because at the present time there is nothing but confusion in the minds of the people.
This tax is restrictive because it hits the manufacturing industry and the construction industry, two of the biggest employers of labour in this country; and let us not lose sight of the fact that the ordinary individual ultimately pays the shot. I would like to ask you, Mr. Chairman, how in the world can you stimulate-trade and provide employment when you put a deterrent in the market place? The construction industry employs well over 600,000 people in this country. Anything that will restrict this industry will certainly lead to more unemployment; and this was the very thing this government gave its pledge to the Canadian people to reduce. Let us take a classic example of a man who was going to build an "L" wing to his house. His family had increased in size and he was going to put two additional rooms in this wing, the construction of which would cost him about $5,000. When this tax was imposed he decided he was not going to build the "L" extension. While it is true that this tax amounts to only a few hundred dollars, to a man measuring his dollars and cents and raising a family it is

quite a sum. This is one tax that makes no exemption and bears the hardest on people with limited income. It so happens that this man is working in a factory which has recently been taken over and which is going to require a lot of new machinery. They will have to pay tax on these new machines, they will have to pay tax on the product they sell, and the fear of one of the men in that business is that when they are through with all this they may have a product priced out of the market, and will not be able to sell what they are producing. If that is the case, Mr. Chairman, then this man will even lose his job. That is the sort of thing which increases unemployment, in a vicious circle.
I do not want to be unjust to the Minister of Finance, Mr. Chairman. I believe he is an honourable gentleman. But we must remember that all the senior members of the cabinet, including the Prime Minister, saw this budget before it came into the house. While the Minister of Finance must bear the brunt of criticism, nevertheless he has my sympathy. Unquestionably he will have the biggest deficit in history, and I do not believe that deficits are worse than mass unemployment. In spite of the promises of the Liberal party in the last election that they would balance the budget, in this day and age where most people buy on finance plans I believe that it is not a bad plan to have deficit financing, if that deficit financing does not go beyond your gross national product and the growth of your country. I think if I were to choose between unemployment and a deficit budget, I would take the deficit budget.
I should like to deal with another feature of this resolution. I find myself asking the question, when a young couple buy a home and make their down payment, which has been decreased as has the interest rate also, if their down payment does not just cover the present tax. In other words, have they any real equity in this house or have they just paid the sales tax? The same thing occurs, in my opinion, in the attempt to stimulate employment by the building of a house in the winter months. I think you will agree with me that building in the winter months in this country raises the cost at least 10 per cent, depending on the area you build in. The government have the audacity to offer a fellow $500 to build a house in the winter time, knowing full well that if he is building a $20,000 house the house will cost him $2,000 more to build. In other words, in effect they are taking $2,000 out of one of his pockets and putting $500 into another.
I should like to touch on another problem which indicates to me a complete lack of
Excise Tax Act
understanding on the part of the present government. This tax will largely destroy the efforts of industry and labour to make themselves more competitive in the export markets. It is a tragedy, when industry and labour have worked so well together in the last few years to make themselves competitive-and Mr. Chairman, they were getting there

that the government in dealing with them now has not shown more leadership and common sense. As I have said before, I sympathize with the Minister of Finance. Money has to be raised, but surely it could be raised in fields which are not so restrictive to employment. For example, I note that the federal government in 1961 raised $110 million on their excise tax on spirits. I do not believe that it would do any particular harm, and certainly would not be restrictive, if they increased these taxes; and there are other fields they could have tapped, in the same way.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I feel that the minister should completely eliminate his tax on building materials for another year at least, if not forever. If he has to go on with it at that time, however, people would have time to become informed and to realize the procedures involved. This would preclude the great uncertainty which now prevails as to this resolution and it would help temporarily to soothe the general revulsion of the man on the street, as well as the anxiety of the stock exchanges. The man on the street believed sincerely that he had voted for a party which would at least bring in sound fiscal and monetary policies.

Mr. Chairman, we have had such sorrowful sounds of melancholia from the other side of the house that I think it would not be amiss if I dropped a word of cheer to these sorrowful gentlemen, these new prophets of doom and gloom that we have sitting across on the other side. It would appear that now the Conservative party is on record as being the party of fiscal irresponsibility; that several large and evergrowing deficits when they were in office were a monument to that irresponsibility; and we now hear them advocating the removal of all taxes and hence, apparently, a larger deficit than even they were able to produce. It would appear that the new philosophy of the Conservative party is: Govern now and pay later. This is a peculiar philosophy indeed for that party which was once the party of orthodox finance. I feel so badly for these lachcrymose and melancholic gentlemen, and in particular for the right hon. Leader of the Opposition who was wailing so mournfully over there this afternoon, that

Excise Tax Act
I would just offer a word of cheer to the effect that they may have noticed that housing starts were up in the month of June.

Mr. Chairman, in speaking to this resolution I should like to express my views and make some reference to how my own area will be affected. Since June 13, when the budget was brought down, I have had many letters and briefs complaining about the taxes it contained. I have discussed the situation with different plant managers and I am at a loss to know why the Minister of Finance feels he is helping the economy of the country and promoting employment. This feeling is non-existent in my riding.
The Minister of Finance said on budget night that in order to encourage employment by reviving private capital expenditure, which he said had lagged so conspicuously for the past six years, he would propose important new tax concessions. Effective on the date of enactment, new manufacturing and processing enterprises located in designated areas of slower growth would be given exemption from income taxes for three years from their inception. He also proposed that such enterprises be entitled to write off new machinery and equipment. Another proposal was that any taxpayer be entitled to write off the cost of new buildings located in designated areas of slower growth at the rate of 20 per cent annum, or in as little as five years.
After these budget statements I would like to ask the Minister of Finance what areas he has designated as slow growth areas, when during the last election campaign most of the Liberal members claimed to have slow growth in their particular areas and, at times, even stagnation
Does the minister feel his area of Davenport is a slow growth area? He said, and I quote: "My own riding of Davenport is a high unemployment area". Just how will he designate these areas? Can he refuse these tax exemptions in his own riding? Can he refuse them in any metropolitan Toronto riding? I would like to know exactly where I stand in my own riding regarding new industry, and what is offered to establish a new manufacturer. In Peterborough we have found that the best expansion does not always come from new industries, but from industries which are already established. But there is no help for them. The hon. gentleman went on to say:
It is intended that the measures I have mentioned so far should provide an immediate impetus to increased activity. Accordingly, new assets must be purchased and new businesses must be certified to have come into existence in the period of 24 months following the initial date of these measures if they are to qualify.

Now, Mr. Chairman, with the restrictions the minister has placed on industry, the tax on machinery, and the tax on building material, how does the government expect any new industry to develop in this country in the next 24 months?
I would like to bring just one instance to the attention of the committee. A small industry in Peterborough employing approximately 75 people saw fit to expand their business, and erected another building last year. They have been disturbed since the budget was brought down because, although they are a Canadian firm with 100 per cent Canadian capital, they feel it would be better to carry out their operation in the United States since 80 per cent of their produce is exported, 65 per cent of it going to the United States. Here is a portion of a letter from them:
Our firm is one hundred per cent Canadian. We have developed the manufacture of machines and consumable items, and export the major part of our output to the United States and other countries, over tariff barriers ranging up to 45 per cent.
The cost of production equipment that we must purchase has always been much higher in Canada than it would be if we were located in the United States. With this, and other disadvantages, working against us in Canada, particularly when engaged in export, the budget proposal to tax the means of production another 11 per cent comes as a distinct shock.
The provisions in the budget for rapid depreciation, while welcome, are only beneficial to firms that are in a secure profit position. We feel that comparatively few small Canadian firms are in that position.
We wish to submit facts pertaining to our business which we feel, indicate the problems and possibilities for manufacturing in Canada. Adversity, if made too severe, will cancel the prospects. Twenty years have been required to develop our business to a profitable level.
The pressing need of our business is to acquire the best available equipment for efficient production and be able to retain sufficient earnings to pay for it, as well as to continue the development of our products.
Our considered view is that the recent turn of events poses a serious situation for us, as well as for many other Canadian manufacturers, and merits your urgent consideration.
This is just one instance, and I doubt very much if there is a single member sitting on the government side who does not have a similar situation in his own riding. How can hon. members opposite go back to the people and claim to support these budget measures when they know they are posing a serious threat to our industrial economy? Small manufacturers who have to purchase production equipment out of Canada have to pay as much as 30 per cent more than in the United States and we find they are exporting to the United States 65 per cent of their output. How can this government expect to expand industry by burdening such companies with an additional 11 per cent tax?' The government should realize that they are:

forcing this type of Canadian manufacturer into other countries to produce. I would like to take the Minister of Finance or his officials to my constituency to discuss the measures they have levied on these particular industries.
The Minister of Finance has admitted in his revised budget that the 11 per cent tax will have an immediate and sharp impact on some industries, and I agree with him. Industries in the export business competing against foreign manufacturers will also feel the 4 per cent tax and they have further increases hanging over their heads in the next 18 months.
All the other letters from Peterborough manufacturers find fault with the 11 per cent tax on building materials, machinery and equipment. I would like to read a few quotations from another letter.
The additional 11 per cent sales tax on building and processing materials and equipment will add great expense to our costs. We are in a competitive market with imported materials and this is not going to make our efforts any easier.
The new additional withholding tax will make it such that our parent company would be reluctant to invest further money in Canada.
As you know in recent years we have expanded greatly in the Peterborough area and we would like this to continue but it does not look possible.
As a Canadian I can quite appreciate the desire to have Canadians participate in the industrial expansion of Canada. However, this isn't practical in all cases and I feel that ours is one of them.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this particular company has contributed much to the economy in our area. In the last four years they have increased production, increased the number of employees, and expanded the company. This tax could be considered as a slap in the face to their efforts.
I have spoken to the manager of one of Canada's largest electrical manufacturers, located in Peterborough. This company is a substantial contributor to the employment and welfare, not only of our community, but of the Canadian economy as a whole. The company has, since its inception, devoted itself to integrating its own interests with the developing Canadian economy. They have carefully assessed and supported Canadian government policies developed in the interests of Canada's growth and employment, in the sincere belief that these were also in the interests of the company. Their policy of reinvestment of earnings in Canadian operations has resulted in an average of approximately 72 per cent of earnings being reinvested in Canadian operations over the past ten year period.
The company's total employee compensation last year of just over $87 million, and its expenditure for materials, supplies and other costs of $163 million, give some indication
Excise Tax Act
of the impact of the company's activities on the total Canadian economy. The money paid employees as well as the money paid to a vast multitude of suppliers throughout all communities of this country, has become an important factor in our industrial life.
The sales tax amendments in the budget are estimated to increase the company's cost as a purchaser by something over $1.5 million a year. In addition, the additional tax that must be collected and billed to customers will reach in the order of $8 million per year.
These budget revisions will add very materially to costs, and industry costs generally, without any improvement in output and will, therefore, reduce the efficiency of Canadian industry significantly at a time when improved efficiency is very much required. In keeping with the government's policies over recent years, they have on their own initiative gone into world markets and expanded their exports very significantly. While this has been done at extremely low margins, they have just managed to compete.
With the recent increase in costs resulting from budget changes they may find it puts them in a non-competitive position and their program would be in danger of failure. This is a paradoxical case in which the government is exhorting them to expand their exports and is at the same time proposing legislation which will inhibit their ability to carry out this policy. Those importing products into Canada will obtain an advantage, in so far as their costs are not increased in proportion to the increase in costs of Canadian manufactures due to these budget proposals.
I should like to emphasize that they recognize and appreciate the need for action to help balance the budget and the need for additional revenue. However, they feel that the additional revenue must come from growth and cannot come from hidden extra costs which are bound to inhibit and actually may seriously destroy the very growth that is needed. They sincerely believe that there is a real question whether increased revenue can actually result from the sales tax amendment in the budget.
With regard to the income tax amendments, they are concerned with the discriminatory nature of these amendments. Over the years reinvestment of a large portion of the earnings of their company has been a major part of their policy and has been a major factor in providing employment in this country and our community. The company has exerted itself to be a good Canadian corporate citizen through its reinvestment policy, through the employment of Canadians on its board of directors, through its expansion of export trade and support of Canadian government policies. They sincerely believe that growth

Excise Tax Act
and employment in our community and throughout this country will be seriously and adversely affected by the budget measures and would appreciate recognition of these views in connection with forthcoming government policies.
I should like to suggest the complete withdrawal of this tax so that industry in this country will again have confidence in the Canadian government and expand as it has in the past six years. This course of action will not only help our manufacturers but will be a boost to the economy of our country, which in turn will give more employment to those out of work. I feel that this is the most important objective that the government should strive for at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to speak at this time but I was prompted to do so by the actions and the words of the last speaker on the government side. This budget reminds me of the poet Browning. Someone asked Browning what he meant by one of his poems and he looked at it and said: "When I wrote that, only God and I knew what I meant but right now only God knows what it means". I think that is the attitude of the Canadian people with regard to this confused budget. I believe it was said this afternoon that the best course that could be taken would be to withdraw the budget entirely or, failing that, to exempt all building materials and production machinery.
It has been intimated that the department is swamped with applications at the present time but when the truth is actually known they will not think they were swamped now because there are many other things that have not come to light yet. I have one case here that I want to bring to the minister's attention involving an order or contract which I think will stand up in court. An order was placed by a Canadian company with an American firm for the production of a piece of equipment known as a self-propelled oil well servicing and workover rig. This order was placed with the American company on May 13, 1963 and was confirmed by the American manufacturer on May 22, 1963. The machine went into production on that date and delivery was to be on June 28.
The total cost of this equipment was in the neighbourhood of $65,000. A deposit was paid making the transaction binding. The purchaser's cheque was deposited by the American firm in the National Bank of Tulsa, Oklahoma, on May 20, 1963. I have a letter here from the manufacturer which states that the order was accepted on May 13 and was secured by a cash down payment. They consider that the order contract was firm and binding on both parties. I also have the can-

celled cheque which was deposited in the American bank on May 20. In other words,
I believe that those with legal minds will say that the company concerned had a fixed price contract.
The Minister of National Revenue stated the following in his prepared statement as recorded on page 1472 of Hansard of June 24 last.
I thought you were not going to speak.
Haven't you fellows said enough tonight already?
We have heard enough.

You have not heard half of what you are going to hear. This is what the minister said:
In order to be of assistance to persons who believe they are entitled to relief because they are a party to a fixed price contract, as explained earlier, the department is willing to examine their contracts if they wish to forward them to the customs and excise division in Ottawa before they go to the work of preparing their refund claims.
In this case the minister's offer of assistance was accepted. The company concerned made representations to the department, through their member of parliament. The final reply from the minister on the subject reads in part as follows, and it is very surprising.
I thought you were not going to speak.
I said I was not going to speak unless I was prompted by you fellows.
You cannot say you were not prepared.

That is right. I am prepared to make you fellows sit still. This is what the minister said in part, in his letter:
The sales tax relieving section of the budget resolutions, presently before parliament, provides sales tax relief to a Canadian vendor selling under a fixed price contract entered into prior to June 14, 1963, signed by the parties thereto and which does not permit the vendor to add the extra tax to his sale price. However, this relief does not extend to persons who import goods for own use even though the importer may have a contract with the foreign supplier.
In other words, the department implies that the contract with the foreign supplier is firm and binding but adds this rider, which I imagine was added by the officials of the department:
-this relief does not extend to persons who import goods for own use-
This is a new angle. I wonder how many other angles are buried in this resolution that will not be unearthed until we start getting letters from our constituents. It will not be

just the opposition members who will be getting them. All you backbenchers on the government side will be getting them too. In so far as opposition members are concerned, all we can do is sympathize with our constituents, but you fellows have to make excuses for the members of the cabinet. I suggest that this is a discriminatory revision, and I do not believe the minister wants to put this type of legislation through.
For example, take the hypothetical case of two purchasers of a like piece of machinery or equipment. One orders through another party and the other orders direct from the manufacturer. Now, the one ordering direct for his own use is charged the additional sales tax, but the one ordering through the third party does not have to pay this tax. In the case to which I have referred, this order that I have here, the additional cost to the one firm that will have to pay, would be in the neighbourhood of $7,000.
I could not find any place in the minister's remarks a statement to the effect that importation for end use was not exempt. I am wondering if this is another bureaucratic decision or regulation. Perhaps I could explain just what I mean by a bureaucratic decision. I have had experience with this department on a number of occasions. I think a reference was made in this committee the other day to farm implements. I think the minister should be very careful of the words he uses in these acts. I have another complaint, Mr. Minister, concerning tuned hand bells, which come under tariff item 696. The answer I got was that it was not a philosophical or scientific apparatus or instrument. If you look at the dictionary, it is considered so there, but evidently not by your officials. I think, in these cases, your definitions should follow the dictionary meaning of these words which you are going to use.
I have said before that these regulations are stronger than the acts we pass in this House of Commons. I say again that the ministers are captives of their own departments in that the officials write these letters and then the ministers sign them. I come back as an example to the first dispute I had with the department concerning agricultural implements. I refer to this tariff item 409f, which is in two parts. There is one item shown thereunder, gravity discharge farm wagon boxes. I tried to get one of these into the country a short time ago, and the only difference was that ours was called a truck box. In the west, they do not use wagons any more. I understand that the French translation of wagon is lorry, but not speaking French I did not know that at the time. Is that not correct? They said it did not come under that item because "wagon"
Excise Tax Act
did not mean "truck". The reason we wanted to import it under this item was that all articles brought under this item had what they called an end user's certificate. However, this truck box could have been used for other purposes. We admit that. If the purchaser was forced to sign an end user's certificate, that would have been fine.
However, the officials would not even allow it under that. We go down a little further and there is another item which says, "all other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery, n.o.p.". I understand these letters mean, not otherwise provided for. It certainly should have come under that. I went to a lot of trouble to try to influence the department as to the definition of "farm implement".
Question, question.

You will get the question. Now, looking at any dictionary I find that an implement is defined as a thing of necessary use in any trade. This might be an education to some of you people. The word "necessary" is defined as those things to the doing of a thing which are reasonably required. Then, I went to the law clerk of the House of Commons. I did not tell him what my problem was, but I asked him to give me a definition of an agricultural implement. He said that anything that is mainly used for agricultural purposes becomes an agricultural implement.
In Funk and Wagnall's ready reference dictionary, implement is defined as a means or agent for the accomplishment of a purpose. In McGoldricks hand book of the Canadian Customs Tariff and Excise Duties, recognized as an authority or guide by Canadian industry, starting on page 267, there is a general heading "Agricultural Implements". This same heading of implements is carried on for seven pages, listing hundreds of items considered as agricultural implements by legal authorities and industry.
Then, I went to the library of the House of Commons and I got all of the legal dictionaries I could find there. I took these definitions to the officials of the department and said, "These are all the definitions I could find." At that time, they did not say no, they are not right. They said, "Look, you go over to the Department of Finance; they are the ones who determine what will go into these tariff items." I went to the department and they said, it is in there. They pointed out these two items to which I have just referred, the steel grain wagon box or the other agricultural implement. I went back to the Department of National Revenue and I told them what the Department of Finance had told me, that it was covered by the tariff. They said, "No it is not." I said that finance thinks it is in here; they put it

Excise Tax Act
in. They said, "Yes, but we have the job of interpreting what finance puts in". I said that I had all these definitions which I had looked up-"Will you not accept one of these"? They said, no.
Do you want to say something, Mr. Minister? I will sit down if you do. Finally, I said to the departmental officials, "O.K., you have me beat; it does not come under any of these headings. I will have to write back and tell my constituents about this. But before I do, I should like you, as officials of the department to give me your interpretation of what these two headings mean. What is an agricultural implement?" They said, "We do not have to do that". In other words, they can just sit there and arbitrarily tell me that all these definitions I have found in these dictionaries do not define agricultural implements. Apparently they have that power and the minister will do nothing at all about it.
I may have a few more remarks to make on this item when the bill comes before the house. I think, however, before the bill comes before the house the minister should give some consideration to withdrawing the budget altogether. He would then stop all this confusion that has been obvious in the committee tonight and during the day. We know there is going to be more confusion after the bill is introduced and after our constituents are confronted with problems such as the ones I have outlined tonight. Just wait until your backbenchers start getting letters from your constituents. I hope you can explain things to them.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, the new Kennedy tax and the 11 per cent Gordon tax are uniting to hit Canadians directly. This leads us to believe that our politicians want for our people the same fate as the world boxing champion had in store for the challenger, that is to knock our people out in the first round.
First round here, first budget of the new Liberal administration, first series of taxes, general retreat under pressure brought to bear by outside forces, general loss of confidence, panic in some cases, rejoicing in others, in short, the ropes of the economical ring choke the contenders, goodwill alone is not enough, they begin to realize that what is physically possible must also be made financially possible.
Lack of money must not prevent progress any more, but how they hesitate before taking a decision, because they are afraid to do wrong to the signs cult. They are busy drawing dollars from everywhere they can

find them before considering making more, because they are afraid that dollars might become less rare, less valuable. If they increase the signs to make it possible to use things, they increase debts at the same time in order to keep the means of decreasing the signs, to prevent the individuals from freeing themselves.
The lift-pump operates in all corners, in all pockets: direct and indirect taxes, increased prices, the taxpayers, the consumers, emptied to the last drop, do not know what to do; government taxes at all levels, bank taxes, trust taxes.
The privileged financier does not even have the trouble of manoeuvering the debentures that cost him only a stroke of the pen and a few accounting operations and that assure him a primary right on the public income. The financier is beaming, he is the first to be served, and in the name of the law too, by the manager of a struggling society, the Minister of Finance.
Joe works, Banco does the business.
Joe pays, Banco picks up.
Joe is deprived, Banco enriched.
Is he not the one who made the required money come out of his ink-stand? When he is about quits with his government, Joe takes a look at his electricity bills, his waterfalls, his mines, his soil and his subsoil, and he wonders what imps have installed such a perfect pumping system, that he does not understand too well but whose existence he is well aware of and which his common sense tells him is undesirable.
Joe looks at his house, his industry, his business, his municipalities, his schools, his bridges, his roads, his universities, his sons who have to set up a family on terms and who have to look up to finance companies for a small measure of respite. Alas, they find only a father who works devoutly for a finance company and who is tied to the latter by a chain whose links he has forged himself. Banco empties the pockets through the respectable offices of the public treasury; and the trusts, which are the offsprings of the fertile banks, get rich because they are crafty, they share a part of their bounty with the big political parties to be sure of continued protection. With those funds, the political parties are able, during an election, to impress and comfort Joe with their eloquence.
This 11 per cent tax is the result of such a financial system. The Minister of Finance was firmly decided to give to the people what they can rightly expect from the government.
The local, provincial and federal governments are faced with problems which impede their action. This disastrous tax will lead to inflation, to an increase in the cost of living,

to the restriction of credit, not to speak of the numerous additional difficulties it will create for both the public and private sectors of production.
According to Hon. Rene Levesque, this tax is a straight punch on the nose; he said that the development of the entire province of Quebec will suffer from it. But some sectors, such as the building industry, are more adversely affected, as shown by the many telegrams we received on the matter. Personally, I got a few dozen telegrams, as many phone calls, as well as letters on the subject.
On the other hand, we can easily be misled by the latest statistics on unemployment. Figures released by the Department of Labour and the d.b.s. show that the rate of unemployment in Canada went down to 4.4 per cent of the labour force in June. It is said to be an increase of 43,000 jobs compared with the previous month. In the province of Quebec, there were 113,000 jobless in June, a gain of 17,000 over the previous month. But this gain does not really mean much when we consider that out of the 113,000 jobs created during that period, 79,000 were for students. This proves that the effects of that tax, as evidenced by the telegrams, are most harmful and make an alarming situation even more serious.
The steady increase of indebtedness at all levels of our economic society makes the picture even darker. According to tentative figures which were provided by the Department of Finance, Canada's public debt was as follows as of March 31, 1963: unmatured debt, $17,961.8 millions; gross liabilities, $24,811.9 millions; net debt, $13,937.1 millions. On the basis of the population figure for April 1963, the per capita distribution was as follows: unmatured debt, $953.08; gross liabilities, $1,316.56 and net national debt, $739.53. The following are only tentative figures concerning the interest paid on the debt in 196263: unmatured debt, $709 millions, and gross liabilities, $882 million. On the other hand, the total amount of money in circulation in Canada compared to the public debt, in March 1963, amounted to 86 per cent of the unmatured debt, 63 per cent of the gross liabilities and 111 per cent of the net debt.
The situation is anything but bright, judging by the statistics which I have just quoted. The increasing burden of taxes of all kinds as a result of which many homeowners lose their homes, farmers their farm, industrialists their industries, irrevocably crush all of us, except those who, on account of their
Excise Tax Act
unlimited power, are indirectly responsible for the levy of these taxes. In the province of Quebec alone in 1962, the apparent losses from bankruptcies, non-summary procedures, namely 543 bankruptcies, amounted approximately to $15,695,662 and losses from 915 summary procedures reached $5,779,801.
The financial incapability of extending social measures, according to genuine needs, and of maintaining them in relation to the increase of the cost of living also results from such a state of affairs. This tax will increase the financial needs of hospitals and educational institutions. Those are all financial problems and cannot be blamed on inadequate means of production. But if the sources of production are ample enough to fiU quickly all the orders, public and private, the source of payment facilities, on the other hand, is soon dried up. The total capacity to produce and the total capacity to pay do not balance, far from it, and that balance will always remain harder to achieve with those new taxes, be they direct or indirect.
So, even before the new taxes, there was a discrepancy between the physical possibilities, which are immense, and the available financial means, which are limited, and that is what brings about conflicts where every one wants his share of an insufficient whole.
If everything that is physically possible were made financially possible, the scarcity complex which sharpens conflicts would disappear, since the production system shows no signs of finding it difficult to meet the demand, wherever it comes from.
Nothing obliges a full-fledged organized community, to gear the use of its vast physical assets to its limited financial assets. Rather, the financial machinery should be geared to the possibilities of implementation.
A financial organization which would faithfully reflect its actual wealth, would provide the means of payment in accordance with the production of all sorts of goods and would withdraw those means of payment only in accordance with the consumption of all sorts of goods. The matter of financial problems would not likely come up any more and the only possible difficulties would concern production, but those do not seem to be a source of trouble today.
It is a crime today to regulate and ration money already in insufficient quantity compared to an affluent production, to let human beings suffer, in order to abide by heartless

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to direct the attention of hon. members to the change in the method of calculating the sales tax on gasoline which was announced in the budget speech. The action proposed is to withdraw a discount heretofore granted for sales tax calculation purposes. Because this was an administrative change which would not require an amendment to the act, no paragraph relating to this measure was placed in the excise tax resolutions. I have come to the conclusion, however, that the implementation of this administrative change should be accompanied by a change in the application of the tax to imports of gasoline and related fuels.
It is considered advisable to license importers of gasoline, aviation fuel and diesel fuel and to require these importers, instead

of paying sales tax on the import price at the time of importation, to pay tax on their selling price at the time these products are sold by the importer or put to his own use. If this is to be done-and it is being done to put them on a comparable basis with domestic producers-the Excise Tax Act must be amended to place the importers of gasoline and related fuels in the same position as manufacturers or producers, for sales tax purposes. Although this is a part of the administrative change that was announced earlier, this step will necessitate a change in the act. It is customary to give notice of such amendments in the resolution, and therefore I wish to bring the matter to the attention of the committee and to ask that an appropriate paragraph be added to the resolution.

I move:
That the following paragraph be added to the excise tax resolution:
"18. Mr. Chairman, in rising to say a few words on this bill I might say that I would describe it as a G-string bill, trying to dress up the body of a budget which is now pretty nude. In discussing this first clause perhaps we could look toward the objectives outlined during the last campaign by the Minister of Finance and other spokesmen for the Liberal party. The present minister of external affairs said that the object would be to create a million jobs in the next five years, and that this object would be obtained. It seems to me that the provisions of this bill will do nothing of the sort but will tend to do exactly the opposite. Hon. members talked of increasing trade, of stimulating a stagnant economy and of balancing the budget. I think this bill which is before us will do nothing of the sort. Certainly some of the provisions are designed to stimulate the economy; but on the other hand the government has done so much to harm the economy that it is very doubtful that it will reach its objective. Indeed, I am reminded of the story a professor tells of a frog, where if you put a frog in a pan and you pour hot water on it, it will jump out; but if you put the same frog in a pan and you start with cool or lukewarm water and keep making the water hotter, it sits there and is roasted. Now that is exactly the position of the Canadian taxpayer. When this 11 per cent tax was placed on him all at once, he jumped out of the pan. Now the government is using a more scientific approach. It is starting at 4 per cent and it tends to make it hotter and hotter until the Canadian taxpayer is roasted.
It is hardly necessary to repeat all that has been said about the harm these measures are doing to the Canadian economy. When I listened to hon. members opposite speaking during the election campaign I was under the impression that they intended to get their increased revenue by expanding the gross national product, increasing the tax base

Excise Tax Act
and so on. I certainly never heard anything during the campaign about increasing taxes. Now it is almost an obsession with them that nothing can be done to expand the economy unless taxation is increased. There was the $500 incentive toward house building in the winter months. There was a lowering of the interest rate and a lowering of the down payment-all positive measures. At the same time, the government brings in measures such as this tax on building materials which will cancel out all the goods which those incentives might have produced.
The hon. member for Lisgar mentioned unorganized territories and I would appreciate it if the minister would take into consideration the exemption of local government districts in the same way as municipalities with regard to sewage and drainage systems. I think there is no reason why people who do not have many of the amenities provided by municipalities should be bearing a larger tax in this respect and for this reason I should like to add my word to the remarks of those who have urged the minister to make this exemption.
What has this budget actually accomplished? First, I think it has created a great deal of uneasiness in the country. It has increased the burden on the average taxpayer. It has done something to destroy incentive as far as housebuilders and others in the construction industry are concerned, and employment is higher than it was last year. Where are all these answers which the Liberal party had to the problems of our economy? They said the economy was stagnating, even though under the previous government there was an increase of 8 per cent in the gross national product last year. This year, despite all the answers the Liberals pretended to have, the gross national product is expected to be less-something like 5 per cent. The measures in this budget have undone a lot of the good which was done by the former government in trying to provide incentives. The national house builders association has told us that the tax will add to the price of a home almost twice the amount by which the industry has reduced the cost in recent years as a result of research into new methods and materials.
I do not think there is anything in this budget which is comforting to the taxpayers of Canada. It all boils down to the bumbling, as it has been called, of the minister-the fact that he did not consult those people who could have advised him properly but that, instead, he brought in these amateurs. I do not think the Prime Minister can escape responsibility for the actions of his colleague. I think responsibility must be placed directly

on his shoulders, along with those of the Minister of Finance and the Liberal party as a whole.
The actions of the minister have brought discredit on the government and his party. I think the people of Canada have lost confidence in the hon. gentleman. I believe that if he had taken the honourable course he would have resigned and made way for somebody who would have taken a new approach towards the problems which face us today. I think the Prime Minister must share some of the responsibility because he did not take the opportunity to shift the minister to a more pleasant post.
I do not intend to hold up this bill for very long. I could read a lot of letters which I have received from my constituents and others but I am sure the hon. member from Kootenay East would object. Besides, I do not think there is any necessity for me to do so because other speakers from this side have already done a very good job in bringing these points of view to the attention of the government and of the people of Canada. All I want to say is this: I hope the government will not compound mistake after mistake. I hope they will adopt some of the structive suggestions which have been put forward by some members of parliament, including, indeed, some which have undoubtedly been made by their own backbenchers. They have some able men over there and I think they should be taken into the confidence of the government and that consideration should be given to their views which, I believe, are not unlike our own on these matters, since they reflect public opinion.
This is a budget which has certainly been bungled, a budget such as we have probably never seen in Canadian history. If the party now forming the government cannot handle the affairs of the country in a much better way, the best thing it could do would be to resign and make way for a government which can. If they are so confident, perhaps they should take these measures before the people of Canada and let them reach a decision.

I rise to say a few words on the first clause. I am reminded that the hour is late and therefore I will perhaps be a little more brief than I would otherwise be. I do not think I will take any more than half an hour.
Oh.

When I heard the tirade which came from the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon I was reminded that those who sit in minority parties in this house must have tough hides. With this statement I will pass

over the comments of some hon. members of the opposition. I will only say that we who sit in minority groups feel in many instances that it is a matter of the skunk saying: "I smell something". The charges and countercharges which are going back and forth across the house make us wonder what the ultimate goal of some of the people in parliament really is. With that, I will leave that part of the business and go on to deal with what I want to say to the Minister of Finance. He has been waiting for some time now for me to make a speech and I do not want to disappoint him too much. I believe the minister said there were three avenues open to him in the raising of revenue, an increase in the income tax, an increase in the sales tax across the board or an increase in the corporation tax. I should like to say to the minister that I do not believe it is necessary to increase taxation at all. I think that what we needed to do was not to increase taxation but to put the unemployed back to work, so that instead of these people being a drain on our economy they would be producers and taxpayers and thereby we would not need this increase in taxation.
I certainly believe that if we continue the concept that the minister has put forward, and I think he is sincere, we are going to pile tax on tax until finally we will find ourselves in a state of collapse, because we will not be able to carry on with increased unemployment and more people as a drain on the public treasury, which is actually the economy, and also be developing a situation where there will be fewer taxpayers. If we are going to solve this problem, surely we must have more taxpayers and fewer people out of work. This is the objective.
Having said that, I believe that a solution to the problem can be found. I think the problem can be met through a public works program that will put people to work. I do not say that all our unemployed people can be employed in this way, but certainly if a number of them can be employed in this way they will become markets, as I said before in another debate, for goods and services to which industry would respond. Therefore we would be getting taxes from these people who were on payrolls and we would also be getting taxes from industry that would be producing the goods to supply the needs of these people. Therefore I think we should be looking in this direction.
I am trying to hurry along. The question comes up: Where are we going to get the money? Where does the money come from? I am going to ask the minister to tell me when he gets up to speak on this matter where money comes from. I would ask him
Excise Tax Act
to explain to the committee in detail where money comes from, and it should not take him any more than about 15 words to do so. I am not telling him but I would hope that he would tell the committee.
I come from bush country and I have seen a lot of trees, but I have never seen money growing on them. If we need more money, I would certainly expect that the minister would be able to tell us where that money is going to come from. When we bring in outside capital, about which we hear so much, we are monetizing our resources. I used to explain this in a neat little hypothetical way, but it brings home the point. I used to draw a picture of a stump and I would ask the individual whether or not he knew what it was. He would say it was a stump. I would then draw a picture of a factory and I would say, "What is that?" He would say it was an industry of some kind. I would say that the stump is what the outside investor sits on while we in Canada build factories and industries with our own hands and our own resources, and after we have built them with our own labour and our own resources the fellow from outside our country sitting on the stump owns them.
This is the point. If we know where money comes from and it takes capital to put our people back to work, surely we do not have to depend on outside sources. Suppose Canada were the whole world. What would we do for money from the outside? There would not be any such money. Surely we must find out where the money is going to come from. I expect the minister is going to tell me where it comes from, but in case he needs a little help I should like to put on the record a few quotations. First of all, I should like to quote from the minister, because at this time I do not know anybody better to quote than the minister himself. This is what he had to say, as found on page 1000 of Hansard of June 13 last:
I wish to say a further word about the relationship between the government and the Bank of Canada. In the last analysis it is the government that must take responsibility for monetary policy ... There can be no misunderstanding on this score.
I was glad to hear the minister say that because it really did my heart good.
At the same time the government recognizes that this does not relieve the bank of its own responsibilities in these matters.
Those are good words. I should like to link them with words of a former governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Graham Towers. They are found in the proceedings of the committee on banking and commerce in 1939, and I refer to page 29 where Mr. Towers had this to say.

Excise Tax Act
It has been quoted before but I should like to do so again. He said:
A government can find money In three ways: by taxation-
That is what my friend over here is working on. Apparently that is as far as he got in reading Mr. Towers' remarks. He just got as far as the first method.
-or they might find it by borrowing the savings of the people-
I do not know whether he has any idea of dipping into them. He has not said so in this debate.
-or they might find it by action which is allied with an expansive monetary policy, that is, borrowing which creates additional money in the process.
We can get money here, it seems to me, but I would hope that the minister would not borrow from the chartered banks. I would hope he would borrow from the Bank of Canada which can do exactly the same thing as the chartered banks if he will only let the Bank of Canada do it. I should like to say here that I am only thinking of borrowing for public account, public capital, and not for industrial capital. I should like to make it clear that we believe we have one of the best banking systems in the world right here in Canada.
In addition, the industrial development bank as it is constituted today is an organization that we should seriously consider replacing with a municipal development bank. Let the banking system look after the needs of industry. Let us broaden our base, if necessary, and that will give industry a better chance to grow. It will give them a little bit of leeway so they can breathe better. I think this makes common sense and I believe that on reflection the minister will agree that this is so. As found on page 238 of the same committee proceedings Mr. Towers had this to say:
When a million dollars worth of bonds is presented-
By the government.
-to the bank a million dollars of new money or the equivalent is created.
So we find that there is a place to get money. Therefore if we can get money so these people can go to work they will become taxpayers and will broaden the tax base so that we will not have to have this tax about which the hon. gentleman is worried. I know he has been worrying about it because there have been a lot of people worrying him about it. I will not say anything more because he has had a hatful of worries. There is no doubt of that. I am not egotistical enough to think what I say tonight is going to make any impression compared with the presentations made to him so far.
Favourable letters too.

I do not think the favourable letters were very many. I am quite certain about that. Otherwise he would not have had the worried look he has had for the last few days. The little stroke of business that took place last week end has helped him somewhat, but that was only a sort of sidelight. We have found out where we can get the amount of money that is needed to put people to work. The amount of money that is needed can be actuarially determined. If, with our computers, we can make mathematical calculations to the extent that we know when the eclipses are going to occur and where they are going to cross the earth, surely we can calculate how much money is going to be needed to carry on our economy in a healthy condition.
This brings me to a consideration of the words "inflation" and "deflation". I believe that the only way to deal with the proposition of money at any time is to deal with it in the light of inflation or deflation. It has been said many times that as Social Crediters we want to get the printing presses going to run off money by the bushel. Well, that is just so much nonsense. No Social Crediter ever had that thought. If he said that he was a Social Crediter, he was only a disguised Liberal or Conservative. We know so well we have to have some balance in connection with the creation of new money. I do not believe the minister will deny the fact that when a chartered bank buys a bond, that is a government bond, it creates the money it uses to buy that bond. I do not believe he will deny that. I think if you transfer the position of the chartered banks to the Bank of Canada, then when the Bank of Canada buys the bond it will create money against the assets, the bond, thereby increasing the money supply.
This practice is the same in Canada as it is in the United States. I should like to put on the record something which has been put on the record before in this connection, but I believe it is worth repeating. Some people do not read the same parts of Hansard. As a matter of fact, I believe few people read it. Robert B. Anderson, secretary of the treasury, was speaking before the Associated Press of New York city on April 20, 1959, and this is what he said:
Now, suppose I wanted to write cheques for a hundred million dollars-
They speak of big money, these fellows.
-starting tomorrow morning, but the treasury was out of money. If I called up a bank and said, "Will you loan me one hundred million dollars at 3J per cent for six months if I send you over a note to that effect?" the banker would probably say, "Yes, I will."

You see, he is a good banker.
"Where would he get the one hundred million dollars with which to credit the account of the United States treasury? Would he take it from the account of someone else? No, certainly not. He would merely create that much money, subject to reserve requirements, by crediting our account in that sum and accepting the government's note as an asset."
So, you see, he created $100 million. He goes on to say this:
"When X had finished writing cheques for one hundred millions, the operation would have added that sum to the money supply. Now certainly that approaches the same degree of monetization as if I had called down to the bureau of engraving and printing and said, 'Please print me up 100 million dollars worth of greenbacks which I can pay out tomorrow'."
Then, we bring in the need for alertness, so far as inflation is concerned. Certainly, we must know that this creation of money will not be so great as to cause a rise in prices. We are under contract today which does not allow the free flow of prices up and down according to the money supply. I think the minister will agree with this. The paper companies on the west coast were accused of having a combine in connection with their prices. However, the investigation went right from the cutting of the log, and the transportation of the log to the putting of it through the pulp plant, and it was ascertained each pulp mill had the same costs all the way down the line. The end price was the same. All these items were under contract prices, so we have a basis of price control by the fact that the costs of these operations of these companies are controlled. We have, therefore, a measure of price control imposed upon us. There is no such thing as the free play of supply and demand.
Now, in so far as this business of writing cheques is concerned, I have handed the minister this piece of paper before. However, he was kind enough not to say anything to me, in case I took it up in this speech. Someone just handed me a note to the effect that the chartered banks have created $5,241 million from January 1, 1955 to July 3, 1963, an eight-year period.
The minister has stated, Mr. Chairman, that he would like to see the time when we could balance our budget. We know that this balancing of budgets is wrong; that is not going to bring prosperity. History tells us that. The United States, for instance, has a debt of $300 billion. Lots of people who call themselves economists will relate this to the gross national product. What they are saying, in effect, is this: If I go out and hew a thousand ties, I must owe somebody for the thousand ties. This is not common sense, but this is what they are trying to tell you. We must expand our money supply through a debt
Excise Tax Act
system, and it is all right to expand it according to the gross national product.
I say to the minister we do not need to go into debt at all for the public capital which is necessary to put these few people I am talking about to work, so that they will become taxpayers and we will be able to take them off the backs of the present taxpayer. We can talk about pensions, portable pensions and all this type of thing. I want to tell you a pension is no good unless there is somebody producing to meet the demands of that pension. We all know that. The fellow who was lost in northern British Columbia and had a lot of money and a lot of time to think, would take these thousand dollar bills out and count them one at a time. He was as hungry as all get out. It did not help him very muct.
We can talk about all kinds of pensions, but if we had inflation, it would rob our pensioners. The type of policy that is being followed here, Mr. Chairman, is one that eventually will rob our pensioners more and more. The cost of living is bound to rise under this structure of taxation. Let us get these people building schools, hospitals, roads, bridges, court houses, wharves, airports, airstrips, trails in the forest for the protection of our forests and so on. Let us do some of these things. Then, we will have an asset for the work they have done, and in return for that asset we will pay them from money that is raised in exactly the same way as we can raise it here. If we insist on increasing the national debt to have prosperity, instead of having it in the manner I have outlined, then I will go along with my friends to the left and say let us do it, and let us get prosperity.
However, let us get away from this taxing ourselves to death. If we carry on in this way we are going to find ourselves taxed to the point where our whole economy is going to collapse. We have to put our men to work. We have to make taxpayers out of them so that they can carry on in the normal way and live a decent life.
I should like to make just one short reference before I sit down, and that is a reference to British Columbia. The other day I whispered quietly to the minister that he should have Bennett over here to talk to him. I see that he has skipped out somewhere and will not be here for the conference. I had hoped he would be here so that we could get together and do something about this matter. I see that, according to the press, British Columbia has a budget surplus of $56 million for last year. Now, this is quite a sizeable budget surplus. I think the Minister of Finance could get some business along that line if he

Excise Tax Act
wanted to use the Bank of Canada. However, perhaps his hands are tied. I cannot see from here, but perhaps his hands are tied.
I shall just quote this and then sit down. We have heard that British Columbia has some sneaky ways of keeping its accounts. Well, Mr. Chairman, the Financial Times of August 7, 1959, had this to say in a first line editorial:
Perhaps the showmanship on the occasion of B.C.'s bond burning last week was extravagant but the achievement was real.
When Premier W. A. C. Bennett of British Columbia, in an elaborate ritualand it was elaborate, I saw it myself
-consigned some $70 million of cancelled bonds to the fire, thus wiping out the balance of the provinces direct debt which stood at $191 million seven years ago, he accomplished something which taxpayers all over Canada wish could be done in the name of their own provinces (and of Ottawa too).
But politics creates strange moods. There has been an extraordinary amount of carping; charges of trickery have been raised and fingers are pointed at the direct or contingent debt of the province. The critics have really made hay out of their disapproval of the Bennett claims, although they are on very poor ground indeed.
There is a difference, a very real difference, between direct and contingent debts; between debts the service of which is a direct charge on all government revenues on the one hand, and debts which are largely, or wholly, self-sustaining, occasionally even self-amortizing, such as the bonds issued by provincial power commissions, toll highway commissions and similar government agencies.
An indirect provincial debt is simply one the service of which is guaranteed by the province in the unlikely event that a power commission, etc., would default on its own obligations.
In times of generally rising government direct debts and the steady growth of interest requirements on such debts, one would have thought that B.C.'s achievement would be greeted with serious interest. However, the fact that it was done by a government that happens to label itself "Social Credit" was enough to bring out venom and ridicule.
It is said that substantial sales taxes were needed to retire the debt. But at least these taxes did have this result. We note very high sales taxes in other provinces (and in Ottawa) without any evidence that a similar result is even contemplated. This is one instance where emulation rather than carping is definitely in order.
Here we have an example of a good province, a real up-and-coming province, a province that is not afraid to tackle the Peace river dam at a cost of $600 million and the Columbia river dam at a cost of another $600 million. It is a province that has got drive and ambition.
In closing I would like to say that if we think we can kill unemployment in British Columbia by our expansion, we know very well we never will. That would be the craziest thought, because everybody wants to come to British Columbia.

The point I want to raise, substantiating the argument raised by the hon. member for Lisgar a few moments ago, is in connection with the installation of sewerage and drainage systems in an area which is not an organized municipality. It seems to me that the provisions are somewhat discriminatory against those areas that at present cannot qualify for a government grant. I am thinking in terms of small villages, hamlets, and in particular farm installations.
In the province of Saskatchewan the present hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam made quite a big issue at one time of the fact that he was going to get rid of the old-fashioned outhouses. He got quite a reputation for that. However since he came to Ottawa he seemed to have lost his desire to get rid of them.
I would like the minister to comment on this particular point because these little villages need more improvements than perhaps some of the larger organized areas, and would be discriminated against if the present tax is left as it is.

I would like to add a few thoughts to what the hon. member for Mackenzie has said in respect to exemptions which apply to municipalities. I know it is unreasonable to assume the budget can be changed to suit everything, but when worthwhile suggestions are put forward we certainly hope the minister will give consideration to them.
At least three quarters of my constituency is composed of areas which are rapidly developing but which are not considered to be municipalities. Many of them are classed as local government districts, and according to the bill these areas will not have the same advantages as organized or recognized municipalities. I wonder would the minister tell us whether these areas, which are already set up under provincial status as local government districts, would be considered in the same light as municipalities in regard to certain exemptions, particularly those relating to sewerage and drainage systems.

On clause 4-Refund, of tax paid on goods for use in sewerage or drainage systems.

pleas made. Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether the minister's advisers could answer this question. I wonder if there is not a point here as to the definition of "municipality". The definition of "municipality" may well be wide enough to include these unorganized areas. What is the definition of "municipality"?

Mr. Chairman, a number of questions have been asked and I would like to hear an answer to some of them. The hon. member for Medicine Hat asked a question, as did other hon. members. Could not the minister answer the questions he has been asked?
What is the definition of "municipality"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I may answer that question first, Mr. Chairman, there is not a definition of "municipality" under this act, because they are different in each province. That may be the reason. As far as I know, there has never been a definition in the act.

For example, we could have in the province of Saskatchewan the situation where the province buys some material and an individual goes to the province to purchase whatever is necessary for the installation of a sewerage system. Would that person be exempt from this tax, or not?

Mr. Chairman, I suggested a few minutes ago that I think the minister can get around all these problems if he will accept the declaration of the province that these materials will be used for municipal

Excise Tax Act
purposes, even though they are used in a local improvement district, or in some provinces what they call a local government district, and so on. In Alberta they happen to be called local improvement districts, but they operate in the same way except they are administered by the different municipal districts rather than the local government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the reason I am hesitant to accept all these suggestions at the moment is that this is really a rather complicated subject. I am grateful for the suggestions, but I would like to have an opportunity to study them carefully before reaching a conclusion. I think the suggestion of the hon. member is a good one to study, but I am just a little fearful that it may have some hooks in it or some complications, and I would like a chance to look into it.

I can appreciate that, Mr. Chairman, but I wonder whether the minister would undertake to answer the questions that have been raised on clause 4 at some stage before this bill is passed through committee and given third reading?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will be glad to do so on third reading, Mr. Chairman.

I think there is a point here, Mr. Chairman, that tomorrow it is our understanding that there is to be a conference between the federal and provincial people on the municipal loans fund. Here, surely, is a perfect opportunity for the ten provinces and the federal government to come to an agreement as to what is a municipality. Perhaps if we stood the clause until we have had the assistance of the provinces, we would make some progress.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I doubt whether at this conference tomorrow the provinces will get down to this question, Mr. Chairman. If they do, I will be delighted.
I thought that was the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is just possible, though, that it will be a short conference, and there are two rather important subjects which have to be considered. If there is any possibility of raising the point the hon. gentleman has mentioned, I will be glad to do that. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I am of the opinion that my hon. friend from Royal (Mr. Fairweather) has raised a very important matter. In fact, if we passed that section as it stands now, we would give the minister the right to define what is a municipality and we would thus encroach once again on provincial jurisdiction, because everyone knows that the municipalities are the creatures of the provinces.

I am convinced that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Favreau), who is listening now, agrees with me. That is why I hold that this important question should be submitted to the federal-provincial conference that will be held tomorrow. I submit that it deserves special consideration, even if we do not go as far as letting that article stand tonight.
(Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 4 carry?

Mr. Chairman, there has been a suggestion that the minister should consider accepting the decision of the province as to whether these places that I have mentioned are to be given the same consideration as will be given to municipalities. I am quite sure that if we could obtain some assurance that a plan of this nature would be adopted, we would be quite willing to go along with it. But I think we would have to have some assurance that some such plan would be adopted for the protection of these various places which at the present time are not considered to be municipalities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have undertaken to study this matter. There will be a record in today's Hansard of all the suggestions that have been put forward. But I do not think I am in a position to give any undertakings. For instance, the hon. member mentioned Thompson as one of these areas. It may be that the International Nickel Company is building the sewerage systems there; I dare say it is, but I do not know. This is the sort of thing I should like to look into before reaching any conclusion.

Mr. Chairman, I can accept that reply to a degree, because to a certain extent this is being done under agreement. But I am quite sure we all realize that this will not continue indefinitely in Thompson. The population is 8,000 now, or somewhere near that figure, and it is expected to reach 20,000 or 25,000. If it remains a local government district, the people are going to have to pay for those additional installations. As I said, this also applies to Snow Lake, Lynn Lake, Churchill, and many of the areas in the Swan river valley which are not municipalities.

It seems to me the subject matter which has been raised with regard to what are referred to as near municipal situations, which apparently in the province of Alberta as well as British Columbia are referred to as local improvement districts, is quite an important subject. My understanding is that certain arrangements covering these things have been worked out. There is an accumulation of experience in the field of municipal winter works programs, which have

also been arranged so that in some cases our Indian reserves have been able to qualify. It seems to me that a simple rearrangement of the drafting of this might make it possible under legal regulations that these matters could be included. As I recall it, it was agreed that we would sit till 10.30 and we have gone considerably past that time now. I think if we were to recess now we can proceed later with the remaining clauses. We certainly got past clause 1 very quickly and the minister should be able to bring in any minor modifications which might be required to meet any objections. Therefore I suggest that we should, to use a colloquial expression, call it a day. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I readily endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Fairweather) and the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau), and I wonder whether the minister would not consider the advisability of replacing the word "declared" which appears in the last line of section 4 by the word "recognized".
By complying with this suggestion, I do not believe that the minister would be making a municipality out of an agency, but on the contrary, he would recognize an agency already established by a province. Indeed, if we read the text as it is drafted, we find there is some danger that this interpretation would constitute an interference in the legislation pertaining to municipalities which comes under provincial jurisdiction, whereas if the minister would recognize the existence of a municipality, it would simply be a recognition in fact rather than the establishment of an agency by right.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the views expressed by the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) and I suggest the amendment he put forth be accepted.
I would suggest, however, that the words "for the purposes of this act" be added. In that way, the minister would not take the place of the provincial authority, for if he incorporated a municipality or declared an agency to be a municipality, in my humble opinion, he would be going beyond his powers.

I know this problem is sticky-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Ten thirty.
Thank you.

speechtext: Shall the clause cr.rry?

Could the minister not accept the definition of a municipality as one 28902-5-1691
Excise Tax Act
which is duly declared to be such by the minister of municipal affairs for the respective province? The municipalities are the creatures of the provinces. A conference is being held tomorrow to iron all this out, and I should like to see a little more leeway. The minister is being sticky on this and I should like to see some leeway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With the greatest respect I am not trying to be sticky. I think we are all feeling a little sticky in this kind of temperature. All I said was that this was a complicated subject, and I should like to take all the suggestions which have been made into account before arriving at a snap judgment.

We are asking for a definition of one word, and responsible ministers are concerned. Rather than take the definition of one of the officials or of the minister, why not consult a specified dictionary? The minister can take a choice and we will accept it. Because there are other words which have not been defined and about which we are going to argue. We have been caught on this before and do not want to be caught again.

Mr. Chairman, this is a complicated matter. Moreover, as someone has called it 10.30 perhaps the minister would consider it overnight and tomorrow come up with a suitable amendment, which would certainly be accepted by us on this side.

The last four lines of this clause have already provided for what we are asking, as far as I am concerned. This is a matter of definition. The last four lines read:
-and for the purposes of this subsection any agency operating a sewerage or drainage system for or on behalf of a municipality may be declared by the minister to be a municipality.
If a province declares a local improvement area, a local government area, or some other area to be a municipality for the operation of that area, I think the minister has made provision here; but we need to have some assurance that we will not run into this problem of definition.
You said "I think" at the end of the sentence.

I agree in part with what the hon. member for Medicine Hat is driving at, but as I read that clause it appears to me that if the words "for or on behalf of a municipality" were deleted, the clause would then read:
-any agency operating a sewerage and drainage system may be declared by the minister to be a municipality.
That wording appeals to me as moving in the direction argued for by the hon. member for Medicine Hat.

speechtext:
Shall clause 4 carry?
